item.title: The 2 words that made the FAA ground stop sound like a cover-up
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The two words were “nothing nefarious.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin repeated them after the Federal Aviation Administration halted all domestic flights on Nov. 13, 2026, amid reported failures in aging air-traffic communications equipment. The phrase was supposed to reassure thousands of stranded travelers. Instead, it introduced the possibility of sabotage or a cyberattack before the administration had publicly explained the hardware failure it said caused the shutdown. That ve
item.content:encoded:
The two words were “nothing nefarious.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin repeated them after the Federal Aviation Administration halted all domestic flights on Nov. 13, 2026, amid reported failures in aging air-traffic communications equipment. The phrase was supposed to reassure thousands of stranded travelers. Instead, it introduced the possibility of sabotage or a cyberattack before the administration had publicly explained the hardware failure it said caused the shutdown.

That verbal blunder, however, was not the central failure. A nationwide ground stop had exposed the fragility of infrastructure responsible for keeping aircraft safely separated, and administration officials spent part of their response making a funding argument without adequately answering the immediate question: What had failed, what had been repaired, and why should passengers believe the system was safe again?

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An assurance that manufactured suspicion

Shannon A. Bowen, a University of South Carolina crisis-communications scholar, told The Conversation that officials initially followed a basic rule of emergency communication: speak quickly and disclose what is known before speculation fills the vacuum.

Mullin then created the speculation himself.

By repeatedly insisting that there was “nothing nefarious” involved, he made nefarious activity a national talking point. Bowen said officials would have been better served by stating the affirmative case they claimed to possess: evidence indicated a hardware failure, not a cyberattack. That formulation would have identified the reported cause and excluded an alternative. Mullin’s wording did the reverse, asking the public to trust a denial untethered from a clear explanation.

Bowen argued that the phrase made the episode sound suspicious even if the only misconduct at issue was mismanagement of the routers behind the air-traffic system. The distinction matters. There is no basis in the supplied reporting to conclude that the shutdown concealed an attack. There is ample reason to scrutinize why officials foregrounded an unnamed menace while leaving basic operational questions unresolved.

The cover-up atmosphere came from the administration’s communication, not reported evidence of a cover-up.

The machinery failed; the briefing shifted to money

At a later appearance, Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy disclosed what they knew and fielded questions, Bowen said. But they also appeared to minimize the disruption and moved into a political case for more infrastructure funding.

The need described was substantial: officials had been seeking at least $30 billion to repair the air-traffic control system. Yet invoking that long-term price tag did not tell stranded passengers what the government was doing that day, whether the defective equipment had been restored, or whether flights then in the air were safer than those operating immediately before the shutdown.

Those were not public-relations niceties. They went to the government’s core responsibility in the crisis. The FAA controls the national airspace; cabinet officials control the federal account of what happened. Travelers do not have access to the routers, the failure logs or the remediation plan. When officials substitute assurances and budget advocacy for concrete operational information, they exploit an information imbalance created by their own institutional power.

Bowen also questioned why malfunctioning equipment could not have been restarted during a less disruptive period if overloaded routers were the problem. She cited a reported 17 failures among 22 routers and asked whether officials could have restricted the shutdown to affected airports instead of stopping domestic flights nationwide. The interview did not establish that either alternative was technically feasible, but the questions expose the gap the administration needed to address: why this remedy, at this scale, at this time?

A foreseeable crisis in an aging system

The administration could not plausibly present the breakdown as an unimaginable bolt from the sky. Bowen pointed to another air-traffic-related ground stop roughly three years earlier, describing it as a warning of larger failures to come.

Duffy reinforced that assessment. Because of the infrastructure’s condition, he said on Nov. 13, “you will have more” ground stoppages. That is a remarkable admission from the official overseeing transportation: nationwide aviation disruption is no longer merely a past failure to explain but a recurring consequence the government expects.

Officials are entitled to argue that Congress must finance repairs. They are not entitled to let that argument obscure executive responsibility for contingency planning, airline coordination and honest warnings to passengers. Bowen suggested advance public notices when a ground stop is under consideration, along with earlier consultation with airlines about reducing the harm. Those measures would not replace modern equipment, but they could keep travelers from arriving at airports for flights the government may prevent from departing.

The disruption reached well beyond business travel. Athletic teams and other groups were stranded; the University of South Carolina marching band was caught in the shutdown, though the school’s football team had already departed. Such examples illustrate the reach of the failure, but the stakes are larger than disrupted schedules. A communications breakdown serious enough to empty the domestic sky is an emergency involving the basic reliability of national infrastructure.

The administration’s most revealing message therefore did not come from Mullin’s clumsy denial. It came from Duffy’s forecast. “Nothing nefarious” may have made the briefing sound like concealment, but “you will have more” described the material consequence: officials expect the system to fail again.

item.content:encoded:
From San Francisco to London, the housing crisis isn’t simply a failure to build. It’s what happens when the people who already have homes are given the political power to keep everyone else out.

Nine Years. Zero Apartments. One Very Important Parking Lot.

In 2017, a developer proposed something apparently outrageous in San Francisco: replacing a downtown parking lot with 495 apartments.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Not demolishing a historic landmark. Not paving over a protected forest. Not displacing hundreds of existing families.

A parking lot.

The property, at 469 Stevenson Street, was supposed to become a 27-story residential tower, complete with affordable housing. The San Francisco Planning Commission approved the project in 2021.

Then came the neighborhood opposition.

A local group appealed the decision. The Board of Supervisors voted 8–3 to overturn the project's environmental certification, citing concerns including shadows on a nearby plaza and potential effects on neighborhood rents.

Apparently, San Francisco had discovered a radical new principle of urban planning:

If housing is too expensive, the solution is to prevent people from building more of it.

The State of California intervened, investigating whether the city's actions violated state housing law. The project was approved again in 2023.

And as of March 2026?

Still a parking lot.

The developer was requesting an extension of its approvals through 2029, citing challenging market conditions and rising construction costs.

Nine years of planning, approvals, appeals, reconsiderations, and political obstruction, and San Francisco had managed to preserve one of its most precious urban resources:

A place to park cars.

Meanwhile, hundreds of potential households remained without the apartments that could have stood there.

Welcome to the wonderful world of NIMBYism.

Not in My Backyard — But Especially Not Near My Property Value

NIMBY stands for “Not In My Backyard,” a term describing people who oppose developments near their homes even when they acknowledge that those developments may be needed elsewhere.

The phenomenon is not exclusive to homeowners, nor is every objection to development illegitimate.

But when housing construction threatens perceived neighborhood exclusivity, the familiar arguments emerge.

The building is too tall. It will create shadows. Traffic will get worse. Parking will become difficult. The neighborhood will lose its character.

And frequently lurking beneath those objections is another concern:

What will happen to my property's value?

Let's be clear about something.

Owning a home gives you property rights. It does not give you ownership of the entire neighborhood.

You are entitled to protection against dangerous construction, unlawful encroachment, and demonstrable damage to your property.

You are not automatically entitled to an unobstructed view forever, unlimited street parking, or a neighborhood frozen at the precise moment you purchased your house.

And you certainly shouldn't be entitled to prevent hundreds of other people from finding housing merely because their arrival might inconvenience you.

That's not the defense of private property.

That's the appropriation of everyone else's property rights for your personal benefit.

It's like an HOA, except considerably worse.

An HOA might fine you because your lawn is two inches too tall.

An organized NIMBY movement can help ensure that hundreds of families never have a lawn, an apartment, or even a front door in the first place.

And the truly remarkable part is that the political system often treats this as responsible civic engagement.

The People Who Don't Live There Don't Get a Vote

Here is the structural defect that makes NIMBYism so effective.

Existing homeowners vote.

They attend neighborhood meetings. They contact elected officials. They organize opposition campaigns. They challenge planning decisions.

But the people who would eventually live in those 495 apartments?

They don't live there yet.

They may be young professionals who cannot afford to move into the city. Teachers commuting from distant communities. Healthcare workers spending hours in traffic. Families sharing overcrowded housing because rents are prohibitive.

Some may already live in San Francisco but desperately need somewhere more suitable.

They are real people with real housing needs.

Yet they are often invisible in the local political process.

The people potentially inconvenienced by new construction are identifiable, organized, and politically influential.

The people who would benefit from it are dispersed, frequently unknown, and poorly represented.

The people who already have housing get to help decide whether the people who need housing will ever get any.

And politicians, naturally, respond to the voters standing in front of them.

This is how a legitimate democratic process can become a mechanism of exclusion.

Not because democracy itself is defective, but because the political constituency affected by a decision is larger than the constituency allowed meaningful influence over it.

The people excluded from a city by its housing policies are still affected by those policies.

They just don't get much of a say.

London: NIMBYism with a British Accent

Perhaps this is simply an American pathology?

Unfortunately, no.

Consider London.

Like San Francisco, London is an economically important city with enormous housing demand and punishing housing costs.

England's planning system provides statutory decision periods of eight weeks for ordinary applications and thirteen weeks for major developments, subject to exceptions and agreed extensions.

Sounds reasonable.

Until we remember that statutory deadlines and actual development timelines are not the same thing.

Local councils consult residents, consider objections, and sometimes refer controversial projects to elected planning committees.

Shadows, traffic, parking, privacy, and neighborhood appearance can all be legitimate planning considerations.

One important distinction, however, is that British planning guidance does not treat a reduction in neighboring property values as a legitimate reason to refuse permission.

Nor do neighbors ordinarily have a direct right to appeal an approval through the planning appeals system. Legal challenges generally concern whether the decision was lawful.

That's an improvement over a system where political opposition can repeatedly reopen approved projects.

Yet London still struggles to deliver enough housing.

Why?

Because even without an ordinary third-party appeal, politically sensitive planning decisions can become slow, contentious, and expensive.

Developers face uncertainty. Local councils face organized opposition. Politicians face homeowners who know exactly whom to blame if something changes in their neighborhood.

Different mechanisms.

Familiar outcome.

Paris: You Can Challenge the Law, Not Simply Your Neighbor's Existence

France offers another model.

In Paris, building projects generally require a permis de construire, assessed against applicable planning rules, building requirements, and heritage protections.

Paris is hardly a paradise of deregulation. Its historical architecture is extensively protected, and construction can be extraordinarily complicated.

However, the system makes an important distinction.

A neighbor who believes a permit is unlawful can challenge it through administrative procedures and the courts. The ordinary period for a third-party legal challenge is two months from proper public display of the authorization.

But an objection must rest on a legally recognized basis.

“I don't want those people living near me” is not, by itself, a planning-law argument.

Neither is “I liked my neighborhood better before someone bought the empty lot.”

France still allows development disputes, and legal challenges can be costly. But the governing principle is worth examining:

The question is whether construction complies with the law, not whether its neighbors find it socially acceptable.

That difference matters.

Berlin: There Is a Rule for That

Germany provides an especially revealing contrast.

Berlin has several construction authorization procedures, including an exemption mechanism called Genehmigungsfreistellung.

For qualifying projects that comply with the applicable development plan and other requirements, construction can generally proceed after one month following submission of complete documentation, provided the authorities don't intervene.

Larger or more complicated developments may require ordinary or simplified permits, technical reviews, and additional approvals.

A 27-story tower does not magically receive approval in thirty days simply because it is located in Germany.

But the underlying philosophy is different.

If a project qualifies under an established set of rules, those rules can provide a relatively predictable path forward.

Neighbors may challenge violations of legally protected interests. They do not possess a general entitlement to stop lawful construction simply because they dislike additional housing.

Germany certainly has housing problems of its own, including high construction costs, financing difficulties, and bureaucratic delays.

The lesson isn't that German bureaucracy is wonderful.

The lesson is that predictable rules are preferable to perpetual political renegotiation.

A developer should be able to determine what is legally permitted before spending years attempting to build it.

And a neighbor's personal preferences should not acquire the force of law merely because that neighbor is loud enough.

Brazil: The City Hall, the Permit, and the Absence of a Neighborhood Referendum

Now consider a system familiar to many Brazilians.

In municipalities such as Santo André, in metropolitan São Paulo, the ordinary approach is to submit construction plans to the municipal authorities for evaluation under the applicable building code, zoning rules, and land-use regulations.

Santo André even operates an electronic licensing system called Obra Fácil.

For straightforward projects, the process can be relatively quick, although approval times vary considerably with complexity. Large developments, environmental restrictions, and neighborhood-impact requirements can introduce additional scrutiny.

Brazilian bureaucracy can be maddening. Nobody seriously needs to be told otherwise.

But there is an important distinction between obtaining municipal approval and asking the neighborhood for permission.

For an ordinary, legally compliant project, the municipality generally doesn't conduct a popularity contest among neighboring homeowners.

The property owner submits the required documentation. The government evaluates the proposed construction.

If the project satisfies the applicable requirements, it can be authorized.

Neighbors retain legal protections against violations and harmful activities. Major developments can require public-impact assessments and consultation.

But disliking a proposal is not ordinarily sufficient to stop it.

Imagine having to ask everyone on your street whether you may build a house on land you already own.

And then imagine that, even after city hall approves it, a neighborhood association can drag the decision back into political proceedings because your house might cast a shadow across someone's favorite afternoon reading spot.

That is the absurdity San Francisco has repeatedly demonstrated.

China: The Opposite Extreme

China provides a very different warning.

For decades, Chinese local governments had strong incentives to expand construction and infrastructure investment.

The results were extraordinary.

Entire districts, vast transportation networks, and enormous residential complexes appeared at a pace difficult to imagine in most Western cities.

Sometimes, however, China built considerably more than local demand could immediately absorb.

Kangbashi, in Inner Mongolia, became internationally famous as a supposed ghost city.

Planned for approximately 300,000 residents, it had around 119,000 in the 2020 census.

Empty residential towers and sprawling streets make compelling television.

But the comparison raises a question that Western housing debates often ignore.

Why is excess housing considered an obvious planning failure, while chronic housing shortages are treated as an unavoidable fact of life?

Overbuilding can be economically disastrous, especially when financed through unsustainable debt or driven by speculative demand.

China's property-sector problems are substantial, and nobody should mistake government-directed construction for a universally successful model.

But a city can also suffer from underbuilding.

One system may create buildings without sufficient residents.

Another may have residents desperately seeking buildings that powerful interests won't allow to exist.

Neither represents sound planning.

Yet only one shortage is routinely defended as protecting neighborhood character.

The Economics NIMBYs Would Rather Ignore

There is another problem with the claim that building more apartments will necessarily make housing less affordable.

It conflicts with a substantial body of economic research.

A 2024 review by Vicki Been, Ingrid Gould Ellen, and Katherine O'Regan, published in Housing Policy Debate, examined recent research into housing supply and rental costs.

The authors found that increasing housing supply generally reduces rents or slows their growth at the regional level, with some studies identifying similar effects in surrounding neighborhoods.

A separate study by Andreas Mense, published in 2025 in the Journal of Political Economy Macroeconomics, found that new housing supply can reduce rents across different market segments.

Why?

Because housing markets are interconnected.

When someone moves into a new apartment, they often leave another dwelling available. Someone else moves into that one, potentially freeing another.

New housing creates chains of moves that can increase availability beyond the newly constructed building itself.

Of course, merely approving expensive luxury apartments will not magically provide decent housing for everyone.

Cities need genuinely affordable housing, subsidized construction, preservation of existing low-cost units, and protections against displacement.

But none of those objectives is served by preventing housing construction altogether.

And here's the particularly ugly part of the 469 Stevenson controversy.

The proposed development included affordable apartments.

The 2023 approval provided for 73 affordable units on-site.

The 2026 extension request sought to reduce the on-site affordable share from 19% to 15%, an unfortunate development that underscores how financial pressures can weaken affordability commitments.

That doesn't mean every dollar of increased construction cost can be attributed to NIMBY opposition. Inflation, financing conditions, labor, and materials all affect projects.

But prolonged political obstruction certainly doesn't make construction cheaper.

And when a development becomes financially impossible, the city doesn't get more affordable homes.

It gets nothing.

Or, in this case, a parking lot.

When NIMBYism Becomes the Law

There is something even more outrageous than homeowners organizing to stop apartment buildings from being constructed.

In much of the United States, they don't even need to organize.

The law has already prohibited the apartments.

Welcome to exclusionary zoning, one of the most effective mechanisms ever devised for creating housing scarcity while pretending to regulate urban development.

Consider Los Angeles.

Under its traditional R1 residential zoning, a property owner is generally permitted to build a single-family house, subject to applicable exceptions. A conventional apartment building, however, is not ordinarily permitted in that same zone.

And the restrictions don't end there.

The standard minimum lot size is 5,000 square feet.

That's approximately 465 square meters.

Imagine owning a perfectly suitable piece of land in a city suffering from a housing shortage, wanting to construct a modest four-unit apartment building, and being told that the law reserves your property primarily for one detached house.

Not because the apartment building would be structurally unsound.

Not because the land is environmentally protected.

Not because the infrastructure cannot accommodate additional residents.

But because the zoning designation says so.

California has begun loosening these restrictions. Since 2022, Senate Bill 9 has permitted qualifying two-unit developments and lot splits in single-family zones, with subsequent amendments expanding and refining the framework.

San Francisco has also begun dismantling some of its restrictions. Its Family Zoning Plan, effective January 2026, allows greater density and taller buildings in designated areas, especially along commercial and transit corridors.

These are welcome changes.

But consider what they reveal.

For decades, American cities legally prohibited people from building the very housing those cities desperately needed.

And this wasn't merely an unfortunate consequence of otherwise sensible regulations.

The historical record is considerably uglier.

In 1917, the United States Supreme Court struck down explicit racial residential segregation ordinances in Buchanan v. Warley.

But racial and economic exclusion did not disappear.

Instead, zoning restrictions became an alternative means of controlling who could afford to live in particular neighborhoods.

Minimum lot sizes. Single-family-only districts. Restrictions on apartments. Minimum building dimensions. Requirements that increased construction costs.

The language changed.

The exclusion continued.

In 1926, the Supreme Court upheld municipal zoning authority in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., helping establish the legal foundation for the restrictive residential zoning that spread throughout the country.

And the consequences were enormous.

A 2024 study from the University of California, Berkeley found that approximately 82% of California's residential land within incorporated jurisdictions was zoned exclusively for single-family housing under the zoning rules examined.

Eighty-two percent.

In a state synonymous with astronomical housing prices, vast portions of residential land were legally reserved for the least space-efficient conventional housing arrangement.

Think about the implications.

You cannot construct enough apartments because the zoning doesn't permit them.

You cannot easily change the zoning because existing residents oppose increased density.

You cannot accommodate the population without expanding outward, increasing commuting distances, infrastructure costs, and dependence on cars.

And when housing prices inevitably soar, politicians solemnly announce that the city is experiencing a housing crisis.

As though the shortage had fallen from the sky.

They didn't merely fail to build enough housing. They wrote laws restricting how much housing could be built.

Now, not every zoning restriction is illegitimate.

Separating hazardous industrial operations from residential neighborhoods is sensible. Protecting floodplains, ensuring structural safety, and maintaining adequate infrastructure are essential government responsibilities.

But preventing a duplex, triplex, or modest apartment building from existing in a residential neighborhood simply because it contains multiple households?

That deserves a much better justification than preserving neighborhood character.

Because “neighborhood character” has an extraordinarily convenient habit of meaning whatever the existing homeowners want it to mean.

And historically, those preferences have not always been innocent.

The particularly bitter irony is that many of the same political voices celebrating property rights and opposing government interference have little objection to government prohibiting another property owner from constructing additional homes.

Apparently, freedom extends all the way to the property line.

And then it becomes someone else's problem.

NIMBYism is bad enough when it takes the form of a neighborhood protest.

It is considerably worse when it has been written into the municipal code.

At that point, exclusion doesn't need angry homeowners standing outside city hall.

It has the force of law.

The Property-Rights Hypocrisy

This is where the American contradiction becomes almost comical.

The United States has an extensive political tradition celebrating private property, individual liberty, and limited government interference.

Politicians regularly lecture the public about the sanctity of ownership.

Until someone wants to build apartments.

Suddenly, private property is everyone's business.

The height of the building. The appearance of its exterior. The number of apartments. The hypothetical impact on somebody else's investment.

And the neighbors who demand government intervention to prevent construction may be the same people who insist that government should stay out of private affairs.

Apparently, property rights are sacred only when they belong to people who already own the surrounding property.

This is not an argument for abolishing zoning, environmental protections, or building standards.

Those rules exist for legitimate reasons.

The public has every right to demand structurally safe buildings, adequate infrastructure, environmental safeguards, and compliance with democratically adopted planning requirements.

But there is a world of difference between enforcing rules and allowing organized groups to manipulate those rules into instruments of exclusion.

A property right that depends on the political approval of every nearby property owner is not much of a right at all.

And a housing policy designed around preserving the comfort of existing homeowners is not a housing policy.

It's an exclusion policy.

Democracy Is Not a Neighborhood Veto

Supporters of extensive neighborhood participation often invoke democracy.

Residents deserve a voice, they argue.

And they do.

But having a voice is not the same as possessing a veto.

A democratic government must consider the interests of everyone affected by its decisions, including people who are not organized into neighborhood associations.

Including renters.

Including future residents.

Including workers who commute from miles away because they cannot afford to live near their jobs.

Including young adults who cannot establish independent households.

Including families who must choose between overcrowding and financial ruin.

When the political process repeatedly elevates the preferences of established homeowners over the housing needs of everyone else, it ceases to function as balanced public planning.

It becomes an institution for protecting incumbents.

And its consequences are not abstract.

Housing shortages increase financial pressure, constrain labor mobility, worsen long-distance commuting, and prevent people from living near employment and essential services.

The price of preserving one neighborhood's preferred appearance is distributed across people who may never have visited that neighborhood at all.

That's the part missing from so many local planning meetings.

The people denied housing don't disappear.

They move farther away, pay more, crowd together, postpone major life decisions, or leave the region entirely.

The costs are real.

They simply don't appear on the neighborhood association's balance sheet.

Stop Giving Parking Lots More Rights Than People

The solution is not to eliminate planning.

It's to restore its proper purpose.

Establish sensible zoning laws. Allow enough density to meet actual housing demand. Require appropriate environmental and safety protections. Build and subsidize affordable housing. Protect existing residents from genuine displacement.

And then, when a project complies with the rules, allow it to be built.

Public objections should be evaluated against identifiable legal and material concerns, not treated as an inexhaustible source of political delay.

Procedures should have meaningful deadlines. Unnecessary duplication should be eliminated. Approval should mean something.

Most importantly, governments should stop pretending that protecting the preferences of existing property owners is the same thing as protecting the public interest.

Sometimes those interests align.

Sometimes they don't.

And when hundreds of people need homes while a politically influential minority wants to preserve a parking lot, public officials should be capable of recognizing the difference.

San Francisco's 469 Stevenson Street development is not merely a story about one failed construction timetable.

It is a demonstration of how a city can acknowledge a housing crisis, approve a solution, obstruct that solution, approve it again, and then watch the economics of construction deteriorate while nothing gets built.

All while claiming to care deeply about housing affordability.

Nine years.

Nearly 500 proposed apartments.

A city desperate for housing.

And the parking lot survives.

The housing crisis wasn't inevitable. The obstruction was a choice.

And the people making that choice already had somewhere to live.

item.content:encoded:
How America’s Health Secretary turned public-health prevention into a budgetary inconvenience — and why Senator Raphael Warnock’s interrogation exposed something more troubling than ignorance.

There is a particular kind of institutional danger that arises when someone is given enormous authority over a subject they do not understand.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Ignorance, by itself, is not the problem. Everyone is ignorant about something. Even the most accomplished scientists spend their careers confronting the limits of their knowledge.

The danger begins when ignorance is combined with power, ideological certainty, and an apparent inability to recognize why expertise matters.

Enter Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the United States Secretary of Health and Human Services.

In September 2025, Senator Raphael Warnock confronted Kennedy during a Senate Finance Committee hearing over proposed cuts to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The exchange recently resurfaced in a video uploaded in November 12, 2026, bringing renewed attention to a confrontation that was already troubling when it first occurred. We criticized Kennedy’s approach to public health then, and the passage of time has done nothing to diminish the significance of what that hearing revealed. This is not an attempt to manufacture fresh outrage over old news. It is a reminder that the concerns raised more than a year ago deserve continued scrutiny, particularly in light of what has happened since.

What followed was a remarkable demonstration of the distance between political talking points and the practical responsibilities of running a national public-health system.

And the most revealing part was not what Kennedy didn't know.

It was how he defended decisions affecting systems whose purpose he appeared not to understand.

The Disease That Barely Exists — Because We Prevent It

Warnock began with rabies.

Rabies is one of the most terrifying infectious diseases known to medicine. Once clinical symptoms appear, the disease is almost invariably fatal.

Fortunately, modern medicine has an extraordinarily effective response: identify potential exposures and administer appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis before symptoms develop.

The United States consequently records very few human rabies deaths annually.

This is an achievement of veterinary medicine, vaccination, surveillance, public-health infrastructure, and timely medical intervention.

Warnock explained that the CDC historically provided round-the-clock expert consultation to clinicians confronting complicated rabies exposures.

He then stated that staffing for this service had been reduced to a single person.

Kennedy acknowledged that he did not know the staffing figure.

Later, Kennedy defended the arrangement by pointing out that the United States experiences only one to three human rabies cases annually. He suggested that a single full-time employee could probably handle that volume.

Stop.

Read that reasoning again.

The Secretary of Health and Human Services used the number of people who develop rabies to estimate the workload of a service intended to help doctors ensure that people do not develop rabies.

It is the administrative equivalent of looking at a fire department, noticing that relatively few buildings have burned down, and concluding that the firefighters must be sitting around doing nothing.

Or looking at commercial aviation, observing that catastrophic crashes are exceptionally rare, and deciding that aircraft maintenance and air-traffic control are unnecessary extravagances.

You cannot measure the value of prevention by counting only the disasters it failed to prevent.

A rabies consultation service does not merely advise physicians treating confirmed human rabies.

It helps evaluate potential exposures, determine whether treatment is necessary, interpret complicated cases, and guide decisions before an irreversible infection occurs.

The relevant workload is not simply the number of fatal human cases.

It includes the consultations and interventions that prevent them.

And Kennedy's response did not address that distinction.

The secretary responsible for protecting American public health was confronted with a question about preventive medical infrastructure.

His answer was a death count.

Congratulations. Your Prevention Program Worked. Now You're Fired.

Warnock articulated the underlying problem with unusual clarity.

CDC professionals, he explained, protect Americans from threats that most people never see.

They receive little recognition precisely because their work prevents things from happening.

This is the central paradox of successful public health.

Averted epidemics do not generate dramatic television footage.

Prevented infections don't produce hospital bills.

Children who never contract preventable diseases don't make the evening news.

And the family whose physician received expert advice after a suspicious animal bite may never realize how important that consultation was.

Successful prevention is largely invisible.

That invisibility makes it politically vulnerable.

The people responsible for preventing disasters can be made to look expendable precisely because they have been effective.

An administrator who understands the system recognizes this problem.

An administrator who doesn't may mistake low mortality for low workload.

And a government determined to advertise budget cuts can transform that misunderstanding into policy.

The absence of catastrophe is not evidence that safeguards are unnecessary. It may be evidence that the safeguards are working.

Prions, Hunters, and the Curious Economics of Catastrophe

Warnock moved to another subject: prion diseases.

These are devastating neurological illnesses caused by misfolded proteins. They include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and its variant associated with bovine spongiform encephalopathy.

They also include diseases affecting animals, such as chronic wasting disease in deer and elk.

Human prion diseases are rare, generally fatal, and exceptionally difficult to treat.

Warnock described the importance of the CDC's prion surveillance work and challenged a budget proposal affecting the office responsible for it.

Kennedy again emphasized rarity.

He also cited federal debt and the need for agency-wide spending reductions.

Now, government budgets are legitimate subjects for scrutiny. Every public institution should be able to explain what it does, how much it costs, and whether its programs are effective.

But there is a difference between eliminating waste and eliminating expertise that exists to detect rare but potentially catastrophic threats.

A surveillance program does not become pointless because the disease it monitors is uncommon.

Indeed, rare diseases often require specialized centralized expertise precisely because ordinary healthcare facilities encounter them so infrequently.

A physician might spend an entire career without seeing a particular prion disease.

That makes a national reference and surveillance capability more valuable, not less.

And the apparent argument that a disease is too rare to deserve attention becomes particularly troubling when that disease is invariably fatal.

Public-health priorities certainly require judgments about probability, severity, cost, and opportunity.

But those judgments require evidence.

They cannot be replaced with a shrug and an observation that the disease doesn't happen very often.

You Don't Have to Know Everything. You Have to Know Whom to Listen To.

Let's dispense with one possible defense of Kennedy.

No, the Secretary of Health and Human Services does not need a medical degree.

No, the secretary does not need to memorize every organizational chart across the CDC, NIH, FDA, and the rest of the federal healthcare bureaucracy.

And no, failing to recall the name of a specialized office during a Senate hearing does not, by itself, establish that someone cannot administer a department.

The job is not a medical trivia competition.

It is an executive leadership position.

The secretary must understand what the department's institutions do, what resources they require, what consequences follow from changing their operations, and how to incorporate specialized advice into decisions.

Most importantly, the secretary must understand the difference between personal conviction and scientific evidence.

Kennedy's testimony raises a serious question about those responsibilities.

When confronted with concerns about specialized functions, he did not supply convincing workload analyses or explain how the affected services would retain their capabilities.

He emphasized financial constraints and the relative rarity of the diseases.

The hearing cannot establish how much time Kennedy privately spends studying departmental operations.

But his public responses are fair evidence by which to judge how he explains and defends his decisions.

And the difference matters.

An executive can learn an unfamiliar subject.

An executive can consult specialists.

An executive can revise a mistaken assumption.

What an executive cannot responsibly do is treat specialized public-health functions as expendable without adequately accounting for the work those functions perform.

That is not a dispute about medical credentials.

It is a dispute about the obligations of leadership.

When Scientists Become Obstacles

The controversy becomes more serious when we leave the budget hearing and examine what happened inside the CDC itself.

In August 2025, CDC Director Susan Monarez was removed after only weeks in her position.

During testimony before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee on September 17, Monarez described an extraordinary confrontation with Kennedy.

According to her sworn testimony, Kennedy demanded that she agree in advance to approve recommendations from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, regardless of the scientific evidence.

She also testified that he directed her to dismiss career officials responsible for vaccine policy without cause.

Monarez refused.

Kennedy disputed her account of the demand for advance approval. His department challenged her characterization of the events.

But Kennedy acknowledged during the earlier Warnock exchange that he had demanded the dismissal of career scientists or public-health experts.

Consider the implications of Monarez's allegation.

Scientific review is supposed to examine evidence and then determine whether a recommendation is supported.

Precommitting to a recommendation before reviewing the evidence reverses that process.

It turns scientific evaluation into a ceremonial endorsement of a decision already made.

Under such an arrangement, an independent scientist becomes inconvenient precisely when they perform the job correctly.

The difference between scientific leadership and ideological control is not whether leaders ever disagree with their experts.

Disagreement can be productive.

The difference is whether evidence retains the power to change the decision.

If an administrator has already decided what the scientists must conclude, the scientific process has been reduced to theater.

And if scientists who refuse to cooperate can be removed, the consequences extend far beyond a single personnel dispute.

Science does not become more trustworthy when the people responsible for reviewing evidence are expected to agree with their political superiors before seeing it.

The Institution He Leads Is the Institution He Attacks

Then there is Kennedy's extraordinary description of the CDC itself.

During Warnock's questioning, Kennedy was asked whether he had characterized the CDC as the most corrupt federal agency in the history of the world.

He denied using that precise formulation.

He then said that he regarded it as the most corrupt agency within HHS, and perhaps within the federal government.

This is a remarkable assessment from the person responsible for overseeing the institution.

Of course, federal agencies are not sacred. They can make mistakes. They can become bureaucratic, inefficient, or resistant to legitimate criticism.

The CDC, like any institution, should be subjected to rigorous oversight.

But allegations of institutional corruption require evidence, specificity, and an explanation of what conduct allegedly constitutes corruption.

Sweeping condemnation is not a substitute for identifying actual misconduct.

And it certainly cannot substitute for understanding the functions an agency performs.

Kennedy has framed his changes as necessary to restore scientific integrity and rebuild public trust.

That stated objective deserves to be examined against the actual decisions being made.

If restoring trust means stronger evidence standards, greater transparency, and better accountability, those are measurable goals.

If it means dismissing experienced scientists, reshaping advisory bodies, and demanding adherence to predetermined policy positions, the result is something very different.

It is not enough to declare that an institution has lost credibility.

A responsible leader must demonstrate that the replacement process is more reliable than the one being dismantled.

Otherwise, the word “reform” becomes little more than political packaging.

The Tragedy of Preventable Disease

Near the end of the hearing, Warnock invoked measles deaths among American children.

It was a reminder that public-health decisions are not merely abstract disputes between politicians and bureaucrats.

Measles is highly contagious. Vaccination dramatically reduces the risk of infection and serious complications, while high community vaccination coverage helps prevent outbreaks.

When vaccination coverage declines, the danger increases.

That does not mean every outbreak or death can simply be attributed to a single official. Public-health outcomes emerge from many interacting causes, including vaccination rates, local conditions, exposure patterns, and healthcare access.

But federal leadership helps shape the information, resources, recommendations, and institutional trust on which disease prevention depends.

Those responsibilities carry consequences.

The CDC is not a public-relations operation whose job is to validate the secretary's beliefs.

It is a scientific and public-health institution whose work can determine whether people receive effective protection against dangerous diseases.

Its success depends on evidence, professional independence, and the preservation of institutional knowledge.

Destroying those capacities is far easier than rebuilding them.

A specialized laboratory can be closed with a budget decision.

An experienced epidemiologist can be dismissed with a personnel order.

A surveillance team can be dismantled in an organizational restructuring.

But rebuilding the accumulated expertise, relationships, and systems that made those operations effective can take years.

And pathogens do not suspend their activity while governments reorganize.

Ignorance Is Correctable. The Refusal to Be Corrected Is the Danger.

There is an important distinction between being unfamiliar with a subject and governing as though unfamiliarity imposes no obligation to learn.

The first is an ordinary human limitation.

The second is a serious institutional risk.

A competent decision-making process permits a leader to discover that an initial assumption was wrong.

Perhaps a seemingly expensive department is preventing enormous downstream costs.

Perhaps a rarely used specialist service is essential precisely because emergencies cannot be scheduled.

Perhaps a scientific recommendation conflicts with the administrator's expectations because the evidence supports a different conclusion.

Those possibilities are not embarrassments to be suppressed.

They are reasons to conduct a proper review.

Kennedy's responses in the Warnock hearing provide an especially clear example of what happens when a discussion about public-health capability is reduced to headline numbers.

One to three rabies cases.

A rare prion disease.

A national debt figure.

A mandated percentage reduction.

Each number may be relevant to some part of the conversation.

None, standing alone, establishes that an essential preventive function can be safely dismantled.

What matters is the relationship between resources, workload, expertise, risk, and outcomes.

That relationship was precisely what Warnock was trying to examine.

And it is precisely what Kennedy's responses failed to adequately explain.

The Failure Was Designed

This controversy is larger than one Cabinet secretary's uncomfortable hearing.

It reflects a recurring weakness in political attacks on public institutions.

First, portray specialized government work as bloated, corrupt, or unnecessary.

Then reduce the staffing and expertise that make the work possible.

When the institution struggles, point to those struggles as further evidence that it cannot be trusted.

The process can become self-reinforcing.

A weakened agency is less capable of fulfilling its mission. Its diminished performance can then be used to justify additional cuts.

Meanwhile, the people most dependent on the agency's invisible services may not recognize what has disappeared until they need it.

Nobody wants to discover that a specialized infectious-disease consultation service has been hollowed out while waiting for advice about a potentially fatal exposure.

Nobody wants to learn that surveillance capacity was eliminated after an unfamiliar disease begins spreading.

And nobody wants vaccine recommendations to become a contest between political loyalty and scientific evidence.

The central obligation of public-health leadership is not to make every institution smaller, nor to defend every existing program indefinitely.

It is to preserve and improve the systems that protect the public, using evidence to distinguish what works from what does not.

That demands expertise, humility, accountability, and a willingness to change course.

Warnock concluded that Kennedy should resign or be fired.

That was Warnock's political judgment.

The underlying policy question is broader and more enduring:

What happens when the people empowered to dismantle a prevention system do not adequately account for the disasters that system exists to prevent?

The answer may not become visible immediately.

That is the nature of preventive infrastructure.

Its failures often reveal themselves only after the protections are gone.

And by then, the consequences are no longer theoretical.

item.title: Americans Abroad: When the Land of the Free Discovers the Rest of the World Isn't America
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
Some Americans move to Europe seeking universal healthcare, better work-life balance, and a more humane society. Then they discover that enjoying those benefits might require living like Europeans.

There is a peculiar kind of American exceptionalism that apparently survives even the decision to leave America.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

It is the belief that the United States is simultaneously a deeply dysfunctional society from which one must escape and the universal standard against which every other society must be judged.

The healthcare is broken. The work culture is exhausting. The politics are increasingly authoritarian. Public transportation is inadequate. Social protections are embarrassingly weak for a wealthy nation.

Enough is enough. Time to move to Europe!

And then, upon arrival:

What do you mean people don't do things the American way?

That contradiction is at the heart of a wonderfully revealing video by American expatriate YouTuber Evan Edinger, who examines an October 2026 WIRED article titled “They Fled Trump’s America. Now They Regret It.”

WIRED interviewed Americans who moved to Europe, discovered that their new homes weren't quite the paradise they'd imagined, and began contemplating a return to the United States.

There are legitimate stories to tell about immigration, homesickness, bureaucracy, employment difficulties, cultural exclusion, and disappointment.

Unfortunately, some of the complaints presented offer an entirely different story.

Not one of European failure, but of American expectations colliding with the inconvenient existence of other cultures.

The Dishwasher Crisis: A Tragedy in Two Continents

Consider Annie.

Annie and her husband were in their twenties when they moved from the American South to a town outside London in late 2024. Her husband had received a job offer, and the couple decided to take an adventure.

Before moving, Annie researched British life through TikTok, Instagram, and Reddit.

This is already an interesting choice.

Moving to another country is a consequential decision involving taxation, employment, housing, healthcare, immigration law, transportation, and the fundamental question of how people actually live.

Annie apparently supplemented her preparations with the international-relocation equivalent of reading restaurant reviews.

She arrived expecting charming British suburbs, affordable transportation, excellent healthcare, and the sort of politeness she'd seen in movies.

Instead, she encountered reality.

Among her complaints was that dishwashers and clothes dryers, which she considered commonplace in America, seemed like luxuries in Britain.

Now, Britain certainly has housing problems. Smaller homes, expensive energy, and older buildings can make appliance ownership less convenient than in the United States.

But dishwashers and dryers are not exotic European inventions that have yet to cross the English Channel. They exist. People own them.

Some Europeans also choose not to use dryers because hanging clothes is cheaper, consumes less energy, and can be gentler on fabrics.

Different priorities. Different habits.

But apparently the discovery that British people might dry their underwear without consuming electricity constituted a measurable decline in civilization.

Then came the complaint about having less disposable income.

That's a perfectly legitimate concern. British salaries are often lower than comparable American professional salaries, and housing costs can be punishing.

But the underlying cultural contrast is worth examining.

If your definition of a better life primarily involves purchasing more things, a country that emphasizes different social and economic priorities might indeed disappoint you.

The question is whether the country has failed to deliver quality of life—or whether you've defined quality of life so narrowly that you cannot recognize it when it takes another form.

A society's success cannot be measured solely by how much disposable income remains for the next Amazon delivery.

The Mystery of America's “Smooth” Healthcare

Annie's most interesting complaint concerns healthcare.

She reported difficulties with British National Health Service maternity care and contrasted those experiences with the smoothness of her private health insurance in America.

Evan responded with understandable incredulity.

Smooth?!

American health insurance?!

The system that has turned deductibles, copayments, prior authorizations, network restrictions, and insurance denials into a specialized vocabulary of financial anxiety?

The system in which having health insurance does not necessarily mean you can afford healthcare?

However, there is another possible explanation for Annie's experience, and it deserves consideration.

Perhaps American healthcare was genuinely smooth for Annie because someone else was doing the work.

Under the Affordable Care Act, Americans can generally remain covered under their parents' health insurance until age 26.

Remember, Annie and her husband were in their twenties when they moved.

We don't know her precise age, previous coverage arrangement, or family's financial circumstances. But it is entirely possible that much of her adult healthcare experience occurred while she was still covered by her parents' plan.

Imagine that arrangement.

She visits a doctor. Presents an insurance card. Receives treatment. Goes home.

Meanwhile, her parents might be paying the premiums, handling deductibles, receiving provider bills, reviewing explanations of benefits, and dealing with whatever administrative nonsense the insurer produces.

Depending on the arrangement, she might never have seen most of that paperwork.

To Annie, healthcare would indeed have been remarkably smooth.

Not because the system itself was efficient.

Because her parents may have been absorbing the friction.

Then she moves to Britain, becomes responsible for navigating a different healthcare system, and requires maternity care—potentially more complex than the routine services she previously needed.

Suddenly she encounters delays, bureaucracy, and expenses she cannot ignore.

Her conclusion?

American healthcare was better.

But that conclusion might be confusing a change in the healthcare system with a change in her own circumstances.

There's an important distinction between a system that works well and a system whose failures are invisible to you.

Naturally, this remains a hypothesis. We have no evidence that Annie was on her parents' insurance or that they handled her bills.

And her reported difficulties with maternity care should not be dismissed. Healthcare failures matter regardless of which country commits them.

But the possibility illustrates a much broader phenomenon:

Sometimes what people remember as a system that worked perfectly was simply a system whose failures someone else was quietly handling for them.

But I Pay Taxes!

Annie also objected that British healthcare wasn't actually free because she paid taxes and an immigration health surcharge.

Well, yes.

Public healthcare costs money.

Doctors receive salaries. Hospitals require equipment. Ambulances consume fuel. Medicine needs manufacturing. Someone must pay for all of it.

The distinction is not between healthcare that costs money and healthcare that magically materializes through benevolent government sorcery.

It is between different methods of financing and distributing those costs.

In Britain, NHS services are largely financed collectively, with many services available without a charge at the point of use. Most eligible immigrants also pay an immigration health surcharge, and certain services still carry charges.

In America, healthcare financing combines public programs, private insurance, employer contributions, household premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket payments.

The relevant comparison is not simply how much tax someone pays.

It is how much healthcare costs them overall, what care they can obtain, how quickly they can obtain it, and what happens when they become seriously ill or lose their income.

Annie is right about one thing: British healthcare isn't literally free.

But pointing out that taxpayers fund public services is not the devastating revelation she apparently imagined.

It's how public services work.

American Work Culture Meets People Who Have Lives

Then there is Sarah.

After living in Spain and Edinburgh, Sarah returned to New York, explaining that she missed American outgoingness and the country's characteristic readiness to act.

She described American professional culture as faster-moving, particularly when it came to collaboration and decision-making.

Now, this complaint is not inherently unreasonable.

Slow bureaucracy, indecisive management, and unresponsive colleagues can be genuinely frustrating. Respecting work-life balance is not an excuse for professional incompetence.

But Evan identifies a fascinating contradiction.

Americans frequently praise Europe for its supposedly healthier relationship with work.

More vacation. Greater employment protections. Stronger boundaries between professional and personal life.

Then some arrive and discover that these differences are not decorative features of a European lifestyle brochure.

They influence how people actually behave.

People may not treat every email as an emergency.

They may not organize their identities around their employers.

They may not consider working late an admirable demonstration of personal commitment.

They may even—brace yourself—have plans after work.

There is an interesting cultural assumption buried in the notion that faster automatically means better.

Faster for whom?

The employer? The customer? The employee waiting for a decision? The shareholder expecting quarterly growth?

Speed can be valuable.

But speed is not the only measure of productivity, and productivity is not the only measure of a worthwhile life.

An American employee might interpret a delayed response as insufficient ambition.

A European colleague might interpret the expectation of immediate responsiveness as an inability to respect personal boundaries.

Neither interpretation automatically proves the other culture superior.

But if you deliberately move to a country because you admire its work-life balance, becoming irritated when people actually maintain that balance suggests you haven't fully examined what attracted you there.

You cannot simultaneously demand a society that refuses to live for work and complain that its people refuse to live for work.

Germany: The Terrible Discovery That Freedom Has Boundaries

Then we meet Josh.

Josh moved to Berlin in 2023, partly because of concerns about American politics and the possibility of another Trump presidency.

Unlike Annie, he wasn't entirely unfamiliar with his destination.

He had lived in Germany before. He spoke German. He had friends in Berlin.

Nevertheless, he struggled with finding employment and navigating German bureaucracy.

Those are real problems, and Germany's reputation for administrative complexity is hardly undeserved.

Josh also described feeling like an outsider, arguing that people who weren't born and raised in Germany, and who didn't look German, would never be fully accepted.

That allegation deserves to be taken seriously.

Xenophobia and discrimination do not disappear simply because a country has universal healthcare or better labor protections.

But Josh made another complaint.

He missed American freedom of speech.

And that opens an entirely different discussion.

Freedom of Speech Is Not Freedom From Every Restriction

Germany protects freedom of expression under Article 5 of its Basic Law.

It also places legal limitations on certain forms of expression, including Holocaust denial, particular forms of Nazi propaganda, and unlawful incitement to hatred.

These restrictions exist within the historical context of a country whose previous democratic institutions were destroyed by a movement that used political freedoms to establish a murderous dictatorship.

Germany learned, at an almost incomprehensible human cost, that democratic rights can be exploited by movements seeking to abolish democracy itself.

The principle is straightforward:

Tolerance cannot survive if it is required to grant unlimited protection to organized intolerance.

That does not mean every German speech restriction is wise, proportionate, or beyond criticism.

Nor does Josh's complaint establish that he wanted to express Nazi sympathies or engage in hate speech. He never explained precisely what expression he felt unable to exercise.

But his criticism raises a meaningful question.

What specific freedom did he lose, and why did that limitation matter more to him than the protections Germany provides?

Without an answer, “I miss freedom of speech” is too vague to sustain a serious comparison between two democracies.

The United States and Germany have different constitutional traditions.

One cannot establish that Americans are freer merely by treating the American approach as the only legitimate definition of liberty.

There is another distinction that Americans frequently misunderstand: freedom of speech is not freedom from consequences.

The First Amendment protects your right to express opinions without unconstitutional government interference. It does not require other people to agree with you, respect your opinions, associate with you, or remain silent when you say something objectionable.

You have the right to speak. Others have the right to respond. You can criticize their beliefs, and they can criticize yours. That is not censorship. That is freedom of speech working exactly as intended.

What some people appear to want is not freedom of speech but freedom from accountability: the ability to say whatever they please while demanding that everyone else quietly tolerate it.

And when other people exercise their own freedom to object, suddenly the self-appointed champions of free speech discover that freedom is considerably less appealing when everyone gets to use it.

Escaping the American Right by Moving to… Poland?

And then comes the crown jewel.

Nick, an art director from New York, relocated to Kraków with his Polish wife and their young child.

One of his motivations for leaving the United States was the growth of right-wing populism.

His destination?

Poland.

Poland!

A country with a substantial history of powerful nationalist-conservative movements, bitter disputes over democratic institutions, and deeply contested questions involving abortion, religion, minority rights, and national identity.

Of all the European countries someone might select to escape the political influence of the authoritarian right, Poland is certainly an interesting choice.

Now, to be fair, Nick wasn't choosing a random destination from a map.

His wife was Polish. They had family connections and personal reasons to relocate there.

Those factors matter.

But his subsequent disappointment that European politics were not significantly better illustrates a fundamental misconception about the continent.

Europe is not a country. And it certainly isn't a political ideology.

Sweden is not Hungary.

Portugal is not Poland.

The Netherlands is not Italy.

Different countries have different political histories, institutions, economies, religious traditions, and social conflicts.

Moving to Europe to escape the right without researching the politics of your particular destination is rather like moving from New York to Texas to escape conservative governance because someone told you Austin has excellent coffee shops.

And there's an even larger problem.

Authoritarianism is not an exclusively American export.

Nationalist movements, anti-immigrant agitation, attacks on minority rights, and political efforts to weaken democratic safeguards have their own histories and domestic constituencies throughout Europe.

The American far right may admire, cooperate with, and borrow tactics from European counterparts, but those movements do not exist merely because the United States influences them.

Escaping a political movement requires considerably more research than crossing the Atlantic.

Geography is not an ideology.

Even the Critic Has His Blind Spots

Evan's video is entertaining and often incisive, but not every criticism lands equally well.

For example, he dismisses the employment difficulties of an American influencer who moved to Britain, questioning why she expected to support herself through sponsored content.

There is a reasonable point about researching employment prospects before immigrating.

But content creation is work. Building an audience, securing sponsorships, producing material, and maintaining a business are legitimate economic activities.

One can criticize a poorly researched business decision without pretending the underlying profession isn't real.

Similarly, Annie's experiences with accent-mocking should not be waved away as harmless British banter.

An occasional joke between friends is one thing.

Repeatedly mocking a foreign colleague's accent in a workplace is another.

And an immigrant who feels excluded is not necessarily refusing to assimilate. Sometimes the host society is doing the excluding.

Europe has real problems with xenophobia, racism, class prejudice, and cultural gatekeeping.

Acknowledging those problems does not invalidate the broader criticism of entitlement.

It makes the criticism more precise.

There is a difference between expecting equal dignity and expecting universal conformity to your preferences.

Immigrants deserve respect. They are not entitled to cultural obedience.

The Fundamental Misunderstanding: Comfort Is Not Quality of Life

The most revealing part of this entire discussion is how frequently American expatriates seem to confuse material convenience with overall quality of life.

The United States offers extraordinary conveniences to people who can afford them.

Large houses. Big appliances. Consumer choice. Fast commercial services. Higher salaries in certain professions.

There is nothing inherently wrong with enjoying these things.

But a society's quality of life also depends on factors less easily photographed for Instagram.

Can people afford to become sick?

Can they take time off work without financial catastrophe?

Can they raise children without sacrificing their careers?

Can they move around their communities without owning a car?

Can they maintain friendships, participate in civic life, and spend meaningful time with their families?

Can they retire with dignity?

And perhaps most importantly:

Does a person need to be relatively affluent before those possibilities become realistic?

European countries have not solved all these problems. Some have severe housing crises, strained healthcare systems, low wages, and deteriorating public services.

But their social arrangements often reflect different priorities.

An American accustomed to a large suburban home might feel deprived in a smaller European apartment.

A European accustomed to walking to shops, using public transit, and taking several weeks of paid vacation might regard that same American suburban lifestyle as isolating and exhausting.

Neither perception is imaginary.

The mistake is assuming that one person's accustomed lifestyle represents an objective universal standard.

Moving Abroad Is Not Ordering a Different Version of America

There is another distinction worth making.

Most immigrants do not enjoy the luxury of choosing their destinations based on an idealized lifestyle.

Many move because of war, persecution, economic necessity, family obligations, or the simple absence of viable opportunities at home.

They often arrive knowing perfectly well that life will be difficult.

They learn unfamiliar languages, navigate bureaucracies, accept professional setbacks, and endure separation from family because the alternative is worse.

That doesn't mean wealthier or more privileged migrants are forbidden from complaining.

It does mean there is something particularly revealing about treating cultural adjustment as an unexpected injustice.

When you immigrate, you become the foreigner.

Your accent is different.

Your assumptions are unfamiliar.

Your professional credentials may not translate neatly.

Your habits may be considered peculiar.

Your expectations may not be shared.

And sometimes, despite your best efforts, you won't fit in.

That experience can be uncomfortable, humbling, and occasionally painful.

It can also teach you something valuable.

For perhaps the first time, the culture that shaped you is no longer the default.

You are no longer surrounded by people who instinctively understand your references, preferences, and social rules.

You must confront the possibility that things you assumed were universal are merely American.

And that other people have built perfectly functional lives around different assumptions.

This is not evidence that your new country has failed.

It is evidence that you've moved to another country.

Nostalgia Is Not a Comparative Study

Near the end of his video, Evan makes an important observation.

After more than fourteen years in Britain, he still misses aspects of his American life.

Certain roads in New Jersey.

Familiar restaurants.

Foods he cannot easily obtain in Britain.

Places that carry memories of an earlier life.

And that's entirely normal.

You can miss your childhood home without wanting to move back into it.

You can remember an old workplace fondly without wanting your old job back.

You can miss American conveniences while preferring European social protections.

There is no contradiction.

Nostalgia is an emotion, not an economic indicator.

And immigration is not a referendum requiring you to declare one country superior in every conceivable category.

The most mature perspective recognizes that societies are complicated.

You can admire Britain's NHS while criticizing its waiting lists.

You can appreciate German labor protections while despising its bureaucracy.

You can enjoy American friendliness while condemning the country's healthcare financing.

You can appreciate European public transportation while demanding that rail operators improve service and pricing.

You can even decide that you were happier in America and return home.

None of that is inherently hypocritical.

The hypocrisy begins when you seek the advantages of another society while rejecting the conditions and cultural differences that help produce them.

The Failure Was Designed

What makes these stories fascinating isn't that some Americans regret moving abroad.

People regret major life decisions all the time.

What makes them revealing is the expectation that another society should deliver all the advantages of American life, eliminate its disadvantages, and require no meaningful adjustment in return.

Better healthcare, but without acknowledging how collective financing works.

Better work-life balance, but without accepting that colleagues may prioritize their lives over immediate professional responsiveness.

Better transportation, but without researching actual routes, service quality, or ticket prices.

Greater political security, but without investigating the politics of the destination.

A different culture, but preferably one that behaves exactly like home.

And, naturally, a dishwasher.

The deeper problem is a particular kind of American exceptionalism that persists even among Americans who reject American exceptionalist politics.

They may recognize that their country has serious institutional failures.

They may admire other countries for making different social choices.

But they still approach those countries as consumers accustomed to having their preferences accommodated.

They want to purchase a better society without learning how that society works.

And when reality fails to match the advertisement, they complain that the product was defective.

Yet countries aren't products. Cultures aren't customer-service departments. And immigration is not an all-inclusive vacation package.

There is a world of difference between moving somewhere because you want to experience another way of life and moving somewhere because you expect another way of life to accommodate yours.

One requires curiosity.

The other requires entitlement.

And sometimes the most difficult part of leaving America isn't crossing the ocean.

It's accepting that America was never the center of the universe.

Further reading and viewing

  • Sarah Manavis, “They Fled Trump’s America. Now They Regret It”, WIRED, October 20, 2026.

  • Evan Edinger, “The Americans that Regret Moving To Europe”, YouTube.

  • HealthCare.gov — Coverage for Children and Young Adults Under 26.

  • GOV.UK — Immigration Health Surcharge.

  • Germany's Basic Law — Article 5, Freedom of Expression.

item.title: Trump wrote something mean last night. So what?
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The supposedly “mean” thing Donald Trump wrote is never identified in AlterNet’s dispatch.
