item.content:encoded:
The supposedly “mean” thing Donald Trump wrote is never identified in AlterNet’s dispatch. That omission is the point of its pitch: the latest presidential outburst, whatever it said, matters less than what the outgoing administration can do during the eight weeks before newly elected Democratic majorities take control of the House and Senate.

That is a defensible warning about where power resides during a transition. It is also wrapped in a fundraising appeal that substitutes a cluster of alarming claims for a fully reported account of any particular decision.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Eight weeks of power do not disappear after an election

Voters may have chosen a new Congress, but those lawmakers cannot exercise congressional authority until they are sworn in. The incumbent administration, meanwhile, retains the presidency and the machinery of the executive branch.

AlterNet says fascism scholar Federico Finchelstein and commentator Thom Hartmann warned that a politically cornered lame-duck administration can accelerate its agenda while public attention is fragmented. The outlet points specifically to the elevation of hardliners such as Stephen Miller.

The institutional imbalance is real within the timeline AlterNet describes: future congressional majorities possess an electoral mandate, while current officials still possess the power to issue directives, change enforcement priorities, appoint personnel and reshape policy. An election result does not suspend executive authority for eight weeks. Nor does media fixation on Trump’s online behavior constrain the officials acting under that authority.

That is why treating each offensive post as the whole political event can become a form of misdirection. Trump’s spectacle commands attention; subordinate officials and agencies can produce consequences. The former is easier to broadcast, monetize and debate. The latter requires identifying decisions, responsible officials and the people who will bear the costs.

AlterNet gestures toward the stakes, then passes the hat

The dispatch cites psychiatrist David Reiss’s argument that erratic public displays can function as a smokescreen while officials rewrite federal policy. But the article does not describe a particular policy rewrite. It also invokes former Clinton economic adviser Robert Shapiro’s analysis of the costs of the Iran conflict and a $40 trillion debt, saying those pressures are squeezing programs used by working families.

Those are potentially consequential subjects, but here they serve primarily as evidence for AlterNet’s case that readers should finance more reporting. Publisher Roxanne Cooper says the outlet is seeking $25,000 to expand its reporting staff before the new Congress convenes and had raised more than $8,000 when the appeal was published.

There is nothing improper about an independent newsroom asking readers for money. Reporting costs money, and concentrated ownership by billionaires and private-equity firms creates obvious pressures of its own. But this particular item is an advertisement for journalism framed as the journalism itself. It tells readers that consequential action is occurring behind closed doors, then offers expert warnings and broad policy stakes rather than revealing the action.

The strongest claim in the piece is therefore also an admission: public fixation on Trump’s provocations can obscure the exercise of state power. Yet AlterNet does not resolve that problem here. It uses the same provocation as an entry point, declines to identify it, and redirects the resulting urgency into a donation drive.

The distraction is useful because authority remains intact

The political lesson is narrower than the appeal’s apocalyptic atmosphere and more concrete. An outgoing administration remains an administration. Officials do not lose their legal powers merely because voters have chosen their eventual congressional opponents. If Stephen Miller and other hardliners are gaining influence during that interval, their formal actions deserve more scrutiny than another round of commentary about Trump’s temperament.

But scrutiny requires specifics: which official acted, through what authority, and with what consequence. AlterNet says it wants the resources to provide that reporting. This dispatch does not yet provide it. The unnamed post is noise; the fundraising pitch says power is moving behind the noise. What it leaves readers waiting for is the account of where, exactly, that power moved.

item.title: Trump's DC takeover obsession gets brutal new rebuke from his own base
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s campaign to remake Washington around his tastes has failed to win over even Republican voters. According to Reuters/Ipsos polling reported by The Daily Beast, half of Republicans said new or renovated monuments in the capital were an inappropriate or low priority. Majorities also opposed putting Trump’s name on the Kennedy Center and withholding its funding to force the issue.

The rebuke is not merely aesthetic. It concerns a president using public institutions, federal property and government money to pursue projects centered on his preferences and legacy while his approval rating sits at 32 percent and his party reels from what the reporting describes as a crushing midterm defeat.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Republicans reject the vanity agenda

Across the electorate, 67 percent of respondents considered new and renovated Washington monuments either inappropriate or a low priority. Among Republicans, 50 percent agreed—a particularly stark result because the projects have been promoted by the leader of their party as improvements to the nation’s capital.

Resistance was even clearer at the Kennedy Center. Fifty-three percent of Republicans said Trump should not add his name to the performing arts institution, while 64 percent said it would be wrong for him to withhold federal money until he got his way.

That distinction matters. A dispute over naming can be dismissed as branding or taste. Threatening an institution’s funding turns presidential vanity into leverage: public resources become bargaining chips in a fight to place the incumbent’s name above John F. Kennedy’s.

Trump’s effort to rename the center has repeatedly stalled in court, according to the reporting. Meanwhile, its Trump-aligned board has moved to close the venue for years during a $257 million renovation. Whatever plaque ultimately hangs on the building, the public consequence is already larger than the president’s branding dispute: a major cultural institution is facing a prolonged shutdown.

A capital treated as personal property

Since returning to office in 2025, Trump has pursued a broader physical transformation of the White House and Washington. The most conspicuous project is a huge ballroom being built where the White House East Wing previously stood. Two days after the midterm election, he issued an executive order intended to prevent future occupants from altering his additions to the Oval Office.

That order exposes the governing instinct behind the renovations. Trump is not simply decorating the workspace temporarily entrusted to him. He is trying to bind future presidents to his choices, converting one officeholder’s taste into a lasting federal directive.

Other projects have carried tangible costs. An attempt to give the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool a blue lining reportedly went wrong when the material began peeling and the altered design produced explosive algae growth. Trump has also pursued an enormous “triumphal” arch near Arlington Cemetery. Critics cited in the reporting warn that it would disrupt Washington’s skyline and cast new shadows across veterans’ graves.

Those objections cannot honestly be reduced to elite hostility toward a president’s taste. They concern damage, institutional control and the treatment of nationally significant spaces as a personal design portfolio. The White House, Kennedy Center, Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery do not belong to Trump. His office gives him substantial power over federal priorities; it does not turn the capital into an estate bearing his deed.

Defeat met with more ornament

The timing sharpens the indictment. The Daily Beast reported that Trump retreated further into the renovation projects after Republicans’ midterm losses. Critics accused him of concentrating on the Washington makeover while Americans faced rising living costs, including costs they linked to his continuing war with Iran.

That criticism does not require guessing at Trump’s private motives. His public actions establish the priority: after an electoral repudiation, he moved quickly to protect his Oval Office embellishments from successors. The response was not recalibration but an effort to make his physical imprint harder to remove.

The poll does not show Republicans abandoning Trump wholesale, nor does it establish why individual respondents opposed each project. It shows something narrower and politically revealing: even much of his own coalition does not accept that presidential self-commemoration deserves the government’s attention or coercive power.

Trump still possesses the authority that Republican voters answering a survey do not. Courts can stall him, public opinion can embarrass him and critics can document the consequences, but his administration and aligned boards control the machinery capable of turning preference into demolition, closure, expenditure and decree. The brutal part of the rebuke is not simply that the projects are unpopular. It is that Trump has continued pursuing them after the public—including voters from his own party—made clear how little value they see in being governed as an audience for his monuments.

item.title: Trump's grip on Americans was finally broken by an unlikely source
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Progressive Christianity—not another faction of the Democratic consulting class—is the unlikely force AlterNet columnist Sabrina Haake credits with helping break Donald Trump’s hold on American politics. Her case rests on a reported Democratic midterm victory of roughly 13 points and the success of religious progressives in Republican strongholds, led by Texas Presbyterian seminarian James Talarico. item.content:encoded:
Progressive Christianity—not another faction of the Democratic consulting class—is the unlikely force AlterNet columnist Sabrina Haake credits with helping break Donald Trump’s hold on American politics. Her case rests on a reported Democratic midterm victory of roughly 13 points and the success of religious progressives in Republican strongholds, led by Texas Presbyterian seminarian James Talarico. The electoral result may show a sharp rejection of Trumpism. The claim that faith caused it, however, remains an interpretation rather than an established verdict from voters.

That distinction matters because Haake’s argument is strongest when it identifies a political contest over Christianity itself, and weakest when it treats one sweeping election result as proof that the contest has already been settled.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A Democratic wave with several possible causes

Haake describes the Democratic margin as the second-largest midterm victory since 1942, behind only the 1974 backlash following Watergate. She lists corruption, inflation, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, war, gas prices and attacks on democratic institutions among the possible sources of voter anger.

She also cautions against pretending the cause is already known. Haake says she intends to wait for SSRS exit polling and regards voters’ retrospective explanations skeptically. That restraint undercuts the headline’s certainty: the supplied reporting does not establish that progressive Christianity broke Trump’s grip, only that candidates invoking it succeeded during a major Democratic wave.

The election nevertheless produced evidence of something politically significant. Democrats did not leave religious language uncontested in places where conservative evangelical institutions have spent decades presenting Republican power as the natural political expression of Christianity.

Talarico challenged the religious right on its own ground

Talarico, whom AlterNet identifies as the first Texas Democrat elected to the Senate in 40 years, centered his campaign on a direct moral argument: “Love thy neighbor.” A member of the Texas Legislature and a Presbyterian seminarian who interrupted his Master of Divinity studies to campaign, he used scripture against the state’s entrenched conservative religious politics.

“We as Christians are called to do more than charity,” Talarico told fellow legislators. “We are called to challenge the systems that make charity necessary.” He also opposed legislation requiring the Ten Commandments in public schools, arguing that the measure itself violated Christian principles.

That approach did more than soften progressive policy with religious branding. It disputed the authority of conservative politicians to define Christianity while using the state to impose sectarian symbolism. Talarico’s argument located faith not in compulsory displays but in material obligations to other people—especially those whom political institutions leave dependent on charity.

AlterNet reports that he was part of a broader pattern. Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat in nearly a century to win a Kansas seat in the U.S. Senate, while Axios reportedly identified at least five progressive faith leaders who prevailed in traditionally Republican territory. They included ordained ministers Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James in Iowa. These candidates repeatedly invoked biblical duties toward poor and marginalized people.

The relevant political development is not that Democrats discovered a more appealing vocabulary. It is that candidates in conservative states challenged a religious power structure that has long converted theological claims into electoral discipline.

The megachurch monopoly was never the whole church

For decades, wealthy megachurches and conservative evangelical organizations have enjoyed an enormous advantage in defining public Christianity. Their prominence has allowed a particular political program—hostility toward migrants, punitive social policy and state enforcement of conservative doctrine—to pose as faith itself rather than as one faction’s use of faith.

“The loudest voices that people hear are these megachurches, and they think that’s what we’re all doing,” the Rev. Janet Maykus, pastor of Austin’s United Christian Church, told AlterNet. She described faith as grounded in “justice and kindness rather than doctrine” and said she prays for Christians drawn into white Christian nationalism.

Maykus’s distinction exposes the institutional misdirection. The political religious right asks voters to direct moral scrutiny downward—toward immigrants, poor people and disfavored minorities—while powerful churches, donors and politicians turn cultural fear into organizational loyalty. Progressive clergy are redirecting that scrutiny toward the people writing laws, controlling public resources and deciding whom the state will punish.

That does not make progressive Christianity the sole authentic form of the religion, a theological verdict politics cannot adjudicate. It does mean conservative evangelical institutions no longer get to claim an uncontested mandate from scripture while pursuing policies other Christians understand as cruelty.

Faith can disrupt the machinery without explaining the whole result

Haake places today’s white Christian nationalism in a political lineage running through Richard Nixon’s Southern Strategy, Ronald Reagan’s Moral Majority, the Tea Party and MAGA. Citing an analysis by João Ferreira Dias for the European Center for Populism Studies, she portrays that development not as spontaneous populism but as a political project that brought fringe radicalism into the national mainstream.

She connects that project to Project 2025, describing the agenda as a program that uses culture-war conflict to distract from privatization and the transfer of public wealth. Her language is polemical, and some of her historical claims reach well beyond what the reported election results alone can prove. But the power arrangement she identifies is concrete: cultural grievance mobilizes voters, while officeholders and aligned interests determine policy and distribute material benefits.

Progressive religious candidates interfere with that arrangement because they contest its moral premise. If care for poor people, solidarity with the persecuted and resistance to cruelty can be presented as Christian duties, then the religious right’s political coalition must defend its policies rather than merely declaring them sacred.

Still, an estimated 13-point Democratic victory cannot by itself show that the country has rejected white Christian nationalism, much less that Trump’s influence has been permanently broken. The supplied reporting establishes a large electoral reversal and a cluster of successful faith-centered campaigns. It does not establish how many voters were persuaded by theology, how many were reacting to economic conditions or corruption, or whether the coalition will survive another election.

The more defensible conclusion is narrower and more revealing. Conservative evangelicals spent decades treating Christianity as political property. Talarico and other progressive faith leaders showed that the deed was never theirs—and voters in several Republican strongholds did not punish them for saying so.

item.title: Legal scholars detail ‘last line of defense’ that held up against Trump
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Federal judges blocked the Trump administration’s attempts to seize powers the Constitution assigns to states and Congress, handing it at least 34 defeats in election-related cases and another 28 losses in Justice Department lawsuits seeking complete state voter rolls. According to legal scholar David Wippman and historian Glenn C. Altschuler, those lower courts—not the Supreme Court—became the “last line of defense” against presidential interference in this year’s midterms. That defense held. T
item.content:encoded:
Federal judges blocked the Trump administration’s attempts to seize powers the Constitution assigns to states and Congress, handing it at least 34 defeats in election-related cases and another 28 losses in Justice Department lawsuits seeking complete state voter rolls. According to legal scholar David Wippman and historian Glenn C. Altschuler, those lower courts—not the Supreme Court—became the “last line of defense” against presidential interference in this year’s midterms.

That defense held. The underlying vulnerability did not disappear.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An executive power grab, rejected in court

Writing in The Hill, Wippman and Altschuler said Trump repeatedly tried to extend federal control over voter registration, ballot distribution and vote counting. Those efforts collided with the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which gives state legislatures authority over the “times, places and manner” of congressional elections while allowing Congress—not the president—to alter those rules.

The executive branch may enforce election law. It does not get to rewrite the division of power because the president alleges fraud. Federal judges appointed by Democratic and Republican presidents, including Trump himself, repeatedly enforced that boundary.

The Justice Department separately went to court 28 times demanding complete voter-registration lists from states, according to the scholars, and lost every case. Critics believed the administration wanted the records to construct its own roster of eligible voters. That purpose remains an attributed concern, not an established fact in the supplied reporting. What is established is the administration’s sustained effort to obtain the lists and its unbroken run of courtroom defeats.

Calling this merely an unsuccessful political strategy would obscure the institutional stakes. The president attempted to exercise election powers his office does not possess. The Justice Department supplied the litigation machinery. Judges stopped them.

The judiciary’s split record

Wippman and Altschuler’s praise for the lower courts comes with an indictment of the Supreme Court. They argued that the justices have spent years weakening the ability of elections to reflect voters’ preferences, pointing to Citizens United in 2010 and this year’s Louisiana v. Callais decision.

The pair described Citizens United as unleashing corporate money in politics and said Callais gutted important Voting Rights Act protections. Their larger point is that the federal judiciary did not act as a single democratic safeguard. Trial judges constrained presidential power while the institution at its summit helped create an election system more vulnerable to concentrated money and diminished voting-rights enforcement.

That distinction matters. “The courts held” is too flattering and too imprecise. Particular judges applied a clear constitutional allocation of authority despite pressure from the executive branch. Other judges, wielding greater power and facing fewer meaningful checks, produced the precedents that Wippman and Altschuler say warped the system in the first place.

A California federal court captured the danger in U.S. v. Weber: “the taking of democracy does not occur in one fell swoop; it is chipped away piece-by-piece until there is nothing left.” The administration’s losses prevented some of that erosion. They did not repair what earlier rulings had already removed.

A safeguard is not a governing plan

Wippman and Altschuler warned against making constitutional government depend on individual judges resisting presidential pressure and unsupported fraud claims. That is the central lesson of the litigation record. Thirty-four defeats demonstrate that the legal barrier worked repeatedly; they also show how repeatedly the administration tested it.

The scholars therefore placed the next responsibility on congressional Democrats and their new majorities. They called for limits on partisan gerrymandering, stronger Voting Rights Act protections and regulation of dark money, while acknowledging that some changes may have to wait for a different president or a changed Supreme Court.

That agenda identifies where power now sits. Judges can reject an unlawful demand presented in a particular case. They cannot, through gratitude alone, close the structural openings that invite the next demand. Congress can legislate, but only if its members use their majorities rather than treating favorable court rulings as proof that the system will automatically defend itself.

The lower courts preserved the constitutional line this time. The more revealing fact is that a president crossed toward it over and over, enlisted the Justice Department in the effort, and forced individual judges to become the barrier Congress had not yet built into law.

item.title: Trump official wants to go after a general — but can’t think of a crime
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Pentagon is reportedly exploring criminal charges against Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a senior Army officer Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired last month, even though Sylvia has not been charged and the alleged conduct remains unclear. The sequence matters: Hegseth’s department appears to have selected the man it wants to punish before publicly identifying a prosecutable offense. AlterNet, citing Daily Beast reporting based on The Washington Post, describes the effort as part of an escalating c
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon is reportedly exploring criminal charges against Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a senior Army officer Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired last month, even though Sylvia has not been charged and the alleged conduct remains unclear. The sequence matters: Hegseth’s department appears to have selected the man it wants to punish before publicly identifying a prosecutable offense.

AlterNet, citing Daily Beast reporting based on The Washington Post, describes the effort as part of an escalating campaign against suspected leakers. Sylvia, 54, had served under Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine as the military’s senior official for plans and policy. According to the reporting, Hegseth came to view him as insufficiently aligned with President Donald Trump’s policy agenda.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

That is a political objection. It is not, by itself, a crime.

A prosecution still searching for its case

The Pentagon is reportedly preparing to pursue charges, but the government has not charged Sylvia with anything. The reporting does not establish precisely what information he allegedly disclosed, to whom, or what statute prosecutors believe he violated. Whether a viable case can be built—and whether a conviction would be possible—therefore remains uncertain.

The Justice Department did little to clarify matters. In a statement to the Post, it said only that it has “ongoing investigations related to possible leaks of classified information” and works closely with government partners, including the Defense Department. The department did not confirm that Sylvia is under investigation.

That distinction cannot be treated as a technicality. An investigation into possible leaks is not evidence that Sylvia committed one. A Pentagon effort to make an example of a fired officer is not a criminal case. And hostility toward an official’s perceived politics cannot substitute for evidence of unlawful disclosure.

Hegseth has tried this route before. According to the Daily Beast, an earlier attempt to punish suspected Pentagon leakers stalled after referral to the Justice Department. The reported move against Sylvia suggests that failure did not produce restraint. Instead, the department is again testing whether the machinery of criminal enforcement can be used to reinforce political discipline inside the military.

Loyalty becomes the unstated qualification

The institutional power here belongs to Hegseth. He can remove senior officers, initiate inquiries and place the authority of the Defense Department behind allegations that may follow their targets long before any prosecutor files a charge. Sylvia, already fired, must contend with the reputational and professional consequences of being publicly cast as a suspected leaker while the government has yet to specify what he supposedly did.

The administration’s framing redirects attention from that imbalance. “Leak” carries an assumption of misconduct; “classified information” raises the stakes further. But those labels cannot answer the central factual question still hanging over the case: what conduct is Sylvia accused of committing?

The reported political background makes that absence more serious. If Hegseth turned against Sylvia because he believed the general did not share Trump’s agenda, then a subsequent search for criminal liability demands scrutiny as a possible extension of that loyalty test. The available reporting does not establish that political retaliation is the motive. It does establish a dangerous order of operations: dismissal over perceived disloyalty, followed by an effort to construct a criminal case whose basis remains undisclosed.

Republicans saw the purge and objected

Hegseth’s removal of senior military leaders has drawn criticism even from Republican senators positioned to oversee and fund the Pentagon.

In October, Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker of Mississippi told The Hill that he would not have made the reductions a priority and had received little advance warning. Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins of Maine likewise said the abrupt, large-scale reduction in generals and admirals raised concerns. Collins, who handles both the Pentagon’s emergency supplemental request and its annual spending bill, said she had previously warned Hegseth that removing senior military officials was “deeply troubling.”

She also argued that the removals risked depriving the military of the “talent, dedication and patriotism” of women and people of color, who she said had been disproportionately pushed out.

Those objections expose another feature of Hegseth’s approach: the officials responsible for congressional oversight were apparently informed after the department had already chosen upheaval. Wicker and Collins hold significant committee power, but Hegseth did not treat their scrutiny as a prerequisite. The Pentagon acted; lawmakers were left to register concern.

Sylvia’s case now pushes that pattern beyond removal from office. Firing senior officers over perceived political incompatibility already pressures the military hierarchy toward personal and ideological conformity. Seeking prosecution without a publicly identified offense adds the coercive weight of criminal law. Until the Pentagon identifies evidence and files a charge, what it has is not a criminal case against Brett Sylvia. It has a target.

item.title: Ex-staffer exposes 'sinister secrets' at Trump's Pentagon
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The “sinister secrets” disclosed by John Ullyot are less cinematic and more institutionally revealing: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reportedly excluded Democratic senators from customary pre-confirmation meetings, repeatedly brought his wife into official political settings, and allowed her to scrutinize a prospective Pentagon communications official about handling hostile coverage. Ullyot, a former Trump and Defense Department spokesman now promoting a tell-all book, portrays a Pentagon leade
item.content:encoded:
The “sinister secrets” disclosed by John Ullyot are less cinematic and more institutionally revealing: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reportedly excluded Democratic senators from customary pre-confirmation meetings, repeatedly brought his wife into official political settings, and allowed her to scrutinize a prospective Pentagon communications official about handling hostile coverage. Ullyot, a former Trump and Defense Department spokesman now promoting a tell-all book, portrays a Pentagon leadership operation shaped by partisan insulation, image management and an unusually influential unelected spouse.

Those claims do not establish some hidden conspiracy inside the Defense Department. They describe something more concrete: the management of a vast national-security institution as though it were an adversarial television production, with access restricted, criticism treated as hostility and political presentation crowding into government work.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A confirmation strategy built around friendly audiences

Ullyot served as a deputy assistant to Donald Trump late in Trump’s first term. He returned at the beginning of the second administration as a Defense Department spokesman, tasked by Hegseth with helping create a new communications office. Three months later, he was asked to resign for reasons AlterNet says were unclear at the time.

Appearing Sunday on The Daily Beast Podcast to promote The President Deserves Better, Ullyot said Hegseth departed from the customary practice of meeting senators from both parties on the Senate Armed Services Committee during the confirmation process. According to Ullyot, Hegseth met only with Republicans.

That was a choice, not an administrative oversight. Democratic senators still possessed formal oversight responsibilities, regardless of whether they were likely to support the nomination. Refusing them the same informal access offered to Republicans narrowed the process to politically safer encounters and treated congressional scrutiny as something to evade rather than an obligation attached to the office.

Hegseth also brought his wife, Jennifer Hegseth, to each meeting, Ullyot said. Podcast host Joanna Coles suggested her presence could have made it more difficult for senators to question him about his reported infidelity and allegations of sexual assault. That is Coles’s interpretation, not an established explanation for the arrangement. But it identifies the obvious political effect: a spouse’s presence can turn legitimate questioning of a nominee’s record into an encounter burdened by personal discomfort.

An unelected gatekeeper inside the communications operation

Jennifer Hegseth’s involvement allegedly extended beyond accompanying her husband. Ullyot described undergoing what felt like a hostile or skeptical job interview with her before beginning his Pentagon communications assignment. Her questions, he said, focused heavily on how he would deal with “hostile press.”

The account raises a basic question of authority. Ullyot was being considered for government work on behalf of the defense secretary, yet he says the secretary’s wife—who held no identified Defense Department position in AlterNet’s report—participated in assessing his suitability. Whatever informal influence spouses commonly exert in political careers, interviewing prospective Pentagon personnel moves that influence into the machinery of public administration.

Ullyot offered three possible explanations. He said Hegseth’s limited government experience may have left him unaware that bringing his wife into such settings was inappropriate. He suggested her presence also may have served as a visual rebuttal to reports about Hegseth’s conduct with other women. Finally, he described her as continuing the hands-on role she once held as Hegseth’s Fox News producer, effectively “stage-managing” him.

These are Ullyot’s judgments, not confirmed findings about the couple’s motives. His first explanation is also unusually charitable. A defense secretary does not operate without lawyers, ethics officials, political advisers and career personnel capable of identifying boundaries. If experienced officials objected, Hegseth could overrule them; if they remained silent, that would expose a different failure. Either possibility places responsibility inside the leadership structure, not with some generalized confusion about how Washington works.

The exposé is narrower than its packaging

AlterNet frames Ullyot’s interview as an exposure of “sinister secrets.” The reported material does not justify that billing. It provides no secret defense policy, covert operation or evidence of criminal conduct. What it offers is an insider’s account of poor institutional boundaries and a communications culture fixated on controlling confrontation.

Ullyot’s own position also matters. He is a former administration official who was pushed out after three months and is now selling a book arguing that Hegseth is harming the Republican Party’s image. His criticism is therefore not a rejection of the administration’s political project. It is an argument that its Pentagon leadership is managing that project incompetently.

That makes his account narrower, but not meaningless. The Defense Department’s communications apparatus exists to convey information about an institution with enormous coercive power and public consequence. If its leadership screens officials for their willingness to battle a “hostile press,” limits contact to partisan allies and grants an unelected family member influence over staffing, the result is not merely a bad look for Republicans. It is a public institution being organized around the secretary’s political protection.

The most revealing detail is not that Jennifer Hegseth may have been managing her husband’s presentation. It is that, in Ullyot’s telling, the Pentagon’s formal leadership allowed that private relationship to shape who received access, who faced scrutiny and who helped speak for the department.

item.title: Top pollster uncovers why GOP caught in a ‘trap of their own making’
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Sarah Longwell’s diagnosis is blunt: Republican politicians and right-wing media trained part of the GOP base to treat Muslims as a political menace, and those voters now expect the party to keep feeding them the same hostility. The resulting “trap of their own making” is not a messaging mishap. It is the predictable cost of using marginalized people as instruments of political mobilization. Writing in The Bulwark , the center-right anti-Trump publication she publishes, Longwell said Republican
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Longwell’s diagnosis is blunt: Republican politicians and right-wing media trained part of the GOP base to treat Muslims as a political menace, and those voters now expect the party to keep feeding them the same hostility. The resulting “trap of their own making” is not a messaging mishap. It is the predictable cost of using marginalized people as instruments of political mobilization.

Writing in The Bulwark, the center-right anti-Trump publication she publishes, Longwell said Republican efforts to drive turnout through fear of immigrants and transgender people failed in the midterms described by AlterNet. But the anti-Muslim rhetoric penetrated deeply enough among some voters to create a second problem: Republicans seeking to move away from Donald Trump’s openly racialized politics may find that their own base punishes them for doing so.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The base learned what Republican leaders taught

Longwell’s focus groups found Muslim candidates and public figures becoming objects of suspicion among Republican voters. She cited discussions of Abdul El-Sayed and Vivek Ramaswamy, with Zohran Mamdani also entering the conversation. The particulars varied; the organizing prejudice did not.

That fixation did not emerge independently of institutional power. Longwell pointed to rhetoric from elected officials, including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, and right-wing media figures. Party leaders supplied the threat narrative, media personalities repeated it, and voters absorbed it. Those voters now demand further confirmation that their fear is justified—what Longwell called part of the Republican “Triangle of Doom.”

This matters because political coverage often describes bigotry as something that simply resides within “the base,” as though voters spontaneously generated the party’s agenda and officeholders merely followed. Longwell’s account describes a feedback loop with a clear starting advantage: politicians and media operators possess the platforms, money and authority to decide which groups will be portrayed as dangerous. Once that machinery has worked, those same leaders can cite audience demand as an excuse to continue.

Manufactured fear becomes a governing demand

After the election, Longwell said, more voters who had supported Trump multiple times expressed alarm over Muslims’ influence on election results. A 75-year-old Texan called it “a little heartbreaking” that people who might not have “America’s best interest” could vote, move into communities and change laws.

The voter also invoked elementary-school books, “Muslim politics” and sharia law. The remarks are revealing not because they establish any of those alleged developments—they do not—but because they show how suspicion can erase ordinary distinctions between religious belief, political participation and disloyalty. Citizenship and voting cease to count as legitimate democratic activity when the voters exercising those rights belong to the targeted group.

Longwell reported similar concerns among conservative respondents in Georgia, North Carolina and Pennsylvania. She attributed the pattern to inflammatory statements by elected leaders, while noting that it had appeared earlier and especially in Texas, where Republican officials have pushed anti-Muslim rhetoric particularly hard.

The party’s dilemma is about priorities, not optics

Longwell argues that Republicans now face two politically costly choices. They can keep indulging Islamophobia and repel voters who want attention paid to material concerns such as the cost of living. Or they can reduce the bigotry and risk angering supporters who have been taught to regard it as an urgent issue.

Calling that a “trap” is accurate so long as responsibility remains attached to the people who built it. Republican leaders chose scapegoating as an organizing strategy. The fact that it may now constrain them does not turn them into its victims. Muslim Americans remain the people burdened with suspicion about their loyalty, their votes and their presence in public life.

Nor did the strategy become defensible because the reported electoral payoff failed to materialize. The attempt to generate panic about immigrants, transgender people and Muslims treated vulnerable groups as raw material for turnout. Its failure merely exposed a recurring weakness in grievance politics: propaganda can shape an audience’s demands more durably than it can deliver an election.

Longwell concluded that Republicans hoping to distance themselves from Trump’s “brazenly racist GOP” may discover that base voters will not permit the recalibration. That is the party’s actual predicament. It spent years presenting prejudice as vigilance, then found that some of its voters believed the lesson.

item.title: Trump's reaction to latest scandal exposes how checked out he truly is
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump responded to a nationwide aviation shutdown by saying nothing about stranded passengers and promoting his plan to revive American film production. As the Federal Aviation Administration imposed what The i Paper described as only the third complete ground stop at every U.S. airport, the president offered no public reassurance, explanation or sympathy. At 5:52 p.m. Friday, with the disruption still unfolding, his social-media account instead demanded that the country “MAKE OUR ENTERTA
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump responded to a nationwide aviation shutdown by saying nothing about stranded passengers and promoting his plan to revive American film production. As the Federal Aviation Administration imposed what The i Paper described as only the third complete ground stop at every U.S. airport, the president offered no public reassurance, explanation or sympathy. At 5:52 p.m. Friday, with the disruption still unfolding, his social-media account instead demanded that the country “MAKE OUR ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY GREAT AGAIN!”

That was the reaction the headline gestures toward. But calling the episode merely a “scandal” obscures the more concrete failure: the federal government had taken an extraordinary action affecting millions of travelers, and the official with the largest platform in the country declined to address it.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A president absent from his own government’s crisis

The FAA’s order paralyzed commercial travel and left passengers facing fragmented information at airports, according to The i Paper’s Simon Marks. Trump did not call a television network, contact favored reporters or use Truth Social to tell travelers what his administration was doing. Marks reported that the president made no visible effort to stabilize public confidence in air safety.

Presidents do not personally operate the aviation system, and a televised appearance would not have moved an aircraft. But public communication during a national transportation emergency is part of governing, particularly when the administration’s own agency has halted flights nationwide. Trump possessed the authority, staff and communications machinery to explain the disruption. His silence was therefore not evidence that nobody could speak. It showed that the person at the center of the executive branch chose not to.

The contrast with his post about film production was especially revealing. Trump asserted that actors and producers wanted to return from Canada, Britain, Australia and elsewhere. At that moment, the federal aviation shutdown meant travelers across the United States were struggling to get home at all. The administration’s immediate responsibility was functioning transportation; the president’s chosen subject was an entertainment-industry slogan.

Electoral defeat and executive withdrawal

The aviation episode followed what AlterNet described as a major Republican defeat in the 2026 midterms. Trump, normally relentless in public, had largely stopped discussing the election and the political damage confronting his party.

Earlier in November, New York Times reporter Peter Baker portrayed him as subdued and seemingly detached while Republicans assessed their losses. Trump signed a steel beam for a planned White House ballroom and traveled to Florida for a space-program speech. Those activities did not answer the political setback, just as the film-industry post did not answer the aviation crisis.

It is impossible to establish Trump’s private state of mind from this reporting. Descriptions such as “in denial,” “dazed” or “checked out” remain interpretations of his conduct, not independently measurable facts. What the reported record does establish is a pattern of avoidance: faced first with an electoral repudiation and then with a highly visible failure in national transportation, Trump directed public attention elsewhere.

That matters because presidential communications are an exercise of power, not simply a personality test. Trump has repeatedly used his platform to define enemies, elevate preferred controversies and command news coverage. When he withholds that machinery during a crisis managed by his own government, the vacuum protects the administration from immediate presidential accountability while leaving passengers to absorb the consequences.

The election proved harder to seize than to denounce

AlterNet also reported that Trump had repeatedly suggested before Election Day that he might nationalize elections or otherwise interfere if the results went against Republicans. Yet no comparable effort succeeded after the midterm losses.

Beauregard Patterson, election and voting-rights counsel at the Democracy Defenders Fund, told AlterNet that the structure of a midterm election made reversal exceptionally difficult. Because voters in multiple states were choosing separate House and Senate delegations, the administration would have needed to overturn outcomes across several states at once.

Patterson also pointed to the failure of earlier litigation and attempts to federalize election administration, including an effort involving the Postal Service and rules governing whether ballots would be accepted. In Patterson’s account, those defeats left the administration with few effective tools to take control of the results.

That explanation is more useful than portraying Trump’s post-election quiet as simple bewilderment. The relevant constraint was institutional: dispersed state elections, multiple decisive contests and failed legal efforts limited what the White House could accomplish. The results were not protected by Trump’s restraint. According to Patterson, they survived because the scale and structure of the defeat made subversion far harder.

The same distinction applies to the flight shutdown. Trump’s silence did not remove presidential power from the situation. It removed presidential responsibility from view. Millions of passengers still faced the consequences of an extraordinary federal order while the man running the executive branch advertised a cinematic “Golden Age” and left his own government’s emergency unexplained.

item.title: The only way Republicans can survive the MAGA civil war
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Republican Party’s path out of its MAGA civil war, according to conservative columnist David French, requires the anti-Trump faction to win and the party to restore constitutional limits that Donald Trump’s movement discarded. But that prescription runs into a problem the Republican establishment cannot solve through rebranding: MAGA did not seize power from innocent bystanders. Republican officials repeatedly chose personal power over restraint, then treated the consequences as somebody els
item.content:encoded:
The Republican Party’s path out of its MAGA civil war, according to conservative columnist David French, requires the anti-Trump faction to win and the party to restore constitutional limits that Donald Trump’s movement discarded. But that prescription runs into a problem the Republican establishment cannot solve through rebranding: MAGA did not seize power from innocent bystanders. Republican officials repeatedly chose personal power over restraint, then treated the consequences as somebody else’s fault.

French’s immediate target is the explanation circulating through right-wing media after what AlterNet describes as a midterm wipeout. MAGA partisans have blamed “neocons” for pushing Trump into a damaging war with Iran. Their proposed remedy is not retreat but purification—eliminate the remaining influence of the pre-Trump party and intensify “America first” politics.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

That account conveniently places responsibility everywhere except with Trump, his administration and the movement built around him.

The blame-neocons escape hatch

French, writing Sunday in The New York Times, called the MAGA narrative “idiotic.” Trump’s approval rating, he argued, was already declining before the Iran war. He attributed much of the administration’s collapse among Hispanic voters to its “brutal immigration crackdown,” which he described as perhaps the movement’s defining policy.

That distinction matters. Blaming establishment holdovers casts Trump as a captive of advisers and MAGA as a project corrupted from outside. The alternative explanation is more direct: voters were responding to policies the administration itself pursued, including an immigration crackdown central to Trump’s political identity.

MAGA’s response to defeat also reveals how the movement protects its leadership. Success belongs to Trump; failure belongs to infiltrators, insufficiently loyal subordinates or ideological contamination. Under that logic, electoral rejection cannot discredit the project. It can only justify another purge.

French connected that purge mentality to Stephen Miller’s elevation as White House chief of staff. If every setback proves that MAGA has not yet achieved sufficient control, concentrating more authority in its hardest-line figures becomes the movement’s standing answer.

Constitutional conservatism—and selective memory

French proposed “constitutional conservatism” as the Republican alternative. Drawing on columnist George Will, he defined conservatism as preserving the country’s founding principles, institutions, ethos and Constitution. He argued that this framework could help Republicans reverse Trump’s approach to tariffs, Iran, civil liberties and Russia while reaching voters who have rejected the party.

“Conservatives don’t have to change themselves to oppose Trump,” French wrote. “They simply have to, at long last, be themselves again.”

The appeal is clear, but the phrase “be themselves again” launders the central institutional fact. The people with the power to constrain Trump were not merely commentators debating the proper definition of conservatism. They were Republican officeholders whose careers, committee positions and influence depended on remaining inside the party’s governing coalition.

A return to constitutional language may provide an ideological banner for opposing Trump now. It does not erase the choices that allowed Trumpism to dominate Republican politics in the first place. Nor does it establish that the pre-MAGA party consistently practiced the institutional restraint French now presents as its authentic character.

Cowardice was a governing decision

Anthony Scaramucci, Trump’s former communications director, offered AlterNet a less flattering diagnosis in September. Republican officials, he said, had become “cowards” concerned with self-aggrandizement and personal power.

His evidence was their refusal to remove Trump and their failure to convict him during his second impeachment following the insurrection that Scaramucci said Trump fomented. That is Scaramucci’s judgment, but it identifies the relevant power structure more clearly than a story about an abstract conservative civil war. Republican officials possessed institutional opportunities to break with Trump. They chose not to use them.

Calling that cowardice describes their conduct, but it can also soften the calculation behind it. These officials were not powerless spectators intimidated by an external movement. They held offices, cast votes and protected their positions. Fear may explain those decisions; it does not transfer responsibility for them.

The Republican Party therefore cannot “survive” MAGA simply by changing its vocabulary or blaming a disfavored faction for an unpopular war. French’s program requires a confrontation with Trump’s policies and authority. Scaramucci’s indictment explains why that confrontation has repeatedly failed: the officials capable of waging it have valued their own power more than the constitutional principles they now may need for political rescue.

item.title: The secret hedge-fund conference already courting newly elected Dems
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Newly elected Democrats were already being courted by wealthy interests before taking office. According to AlterNet, Majority Democrats—an organization financed primarily by hedge-fund billionaire Steve Mandel—held an invitation-only “What’s Next” conference in Denver last week, bringing Democratic newcomers together with political consultants while excluding labor, civil-rights, environmental, Black and Hispanic leaders. That guest list is the story. Access was extended to professionals paid to
item.content:encoded:
Newly elected Democrats were already being courted by wealthy interests before taking office. According to AlterNet, Majority Democrats—an organization financed primarily by hedge-fund billionaire Steve Mandel—held an invitation-only “What’s Next” conference in Denver last week, bringing Democratic newcomers together with political consultants while excluding labor, civil-rights, environmental, Black and Hispanic leaders.

That guest list is the story. Access was extended to professionals paid to shape political decisions, but not to major constituencies whose votes and organizing helped produce Democratic victories. The imbalance does not prove that any attendee surrendered a principle. It does show who possessed the money and infrastructure to begin influencing new officeholders immediately.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Influence starts before the oath

Democrats celebrating Senator-elect Scott Colom’s victory in Mississippi and Governor-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins’s win in Alaska face a familiar problem: winning an election changes who occupies office, but it does not dismantle the influence industry surrounding that office.

The newly elected officials were seven weeks away from the reported January 3 congressional swearing-in when AlterNet described the Denver gathering. Yet the contest over their priorities had already begun. Corporations, Wall Street lobbyists, cryptocurrency and artificial-intelligence interests, corporate law and public-relations firms, CEOs and billionaire technology executives do not wait for a new Congress to settle in. Their advantage lies partly in arriving early, offering relationships and policy frameworks before competing constituencies can establish comparable access.

Organizations presenting themselves as representatives of “moderate Democrats,” including Third Way, operate within that struggle over the party’s direction. AlterNet argues that such groups, supported by corporate and Wall Street money, seek to preserve the existing distribution of wealth and power rather than pursue progressive change. Majority Democrats’ conference supplied a concrete example of the machinery involved: concentrated financing, private access and professional political intermediaries.

Calling the conference “secret” risks making discretion itself sound like the central offense. The more consequential fact is not merely that the meeting was invitation-only. It is that money purchased an organized channel to incoming public officials while workers and civil-rights and environmental constituencies reportedly had no seat in the room.

The convenient fiction of the corrupted individual

The usual Democratic postmortem blames particular lawmakers for becoming timid, divided or beholden to donors. Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema serve as ready shorthand for that history. But reducing political failure to defective personalities lets the influence system disappear behind its most visible participants.

New lawmakers enter an institution surrounded by donors, lobbyists, consultants and advocacy organizations with the resources to define what counts as realistic. Those actors do not need to issue crude orders. They can narrow the available choices, supply research and language, confer legitimacy and make policies threatening concentrated wealth appear reckless or electorally impossible.

That is why personal integrity, while relevant, is an inadequate safeguard. Newly elected Democrats may believe they can accept access to wealthy networks without becoming accountable to them. Some may succeed. But the political problem is structural: one side can finance private conferences and sustained professional persuasion, while less wealthy constituencies must fight simply to be heard.

The conference therefore should not be treated as evidence that every participating Democrat has been “bought.” The supplied reporting does not establish that. It establishes an attempted cultivation—and an unequal field on which that cultivation occurs.

Celebration without leverage

AlterNet’s argument places responsibility on the voters and organizers who produced the Democratic victories: electoral support must become continuing pressure after the campaign ends. Franklin D. Roosevelt’s reported response to a voter demanding that he deliver on his program—“Ma’am, I want to do those things, but you must make me”—captures the distinction between holding office and possessing enough political force to govern against entrenched interests.

That principle should not become an excuse for elected officials. Voters are not responsible for rescuing politicians from every lobbyist they voluntarily entertain. Officeholders retain agency over whose counsel they seek, whose money they accept and which promises they abandon. But organized public pressure can alter the costs of those decisions, giving lawmakers a reason to resist influence that otherwise arrives with few penalties.

The same conflict appears in the reported debate over Senate Democratic leadership. AlterNet praises Chuck Schumer’s performance but argues that his longevity and proximity to Wall Street and corporate Democrats make Senator Chris Van Hollen the preferable leader for a more progressive caucus. That is not simply a disagreement over generation or style. It is a dispute over which relationships will shape the party when donor access collides with campaign commitments.

Democratic victories created an opportunity for policy change. They did not settle who will control the winners. In Denver, wealthy interests reportedly began making their case behind closed doors while organized labor and several core Democratic constituencies remained outside. The unanswered question is whether the officials invited into that room will treat such access as one perspective among many—or allow it to define the limits of what their victories are permitted to accomplish.

item.title: Hair, makeup, leaked emails —and the ugly revolt against Trump’s GOP chair
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Republicans are moving against Donald Trump’s handpicked Republican National Committee chairman after the party’s severe 2026 midterm losses, but the revolt is aimed less at Trump’s control than at how his chosen apparatus spent party money. According to an Associated Press report cited by AlterNet, RNC members are seeking scrutiny of expenses that allegedly included hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, while the White House is threatening to withhold fundraising help from dis
item.content:encoded:
Republicans are moving against Donald Trump’s handpicked Republican National Committee chairman after the party’s severe 2026 midterm losses, but the revolt is aimed less at Trump’s control than at how his chosen apparatus spent party money. According to an Associated Press report cited by AlterNet, RNC members are seeking scrutiny of expenses that allegedly included hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, while the White House is threatening to withhold fundraising help from dissenters. The chairman at the center of the dispute is not named in the supplied reporting.

Party money and presidential privilege

Some RNC members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, the AP reported. Their complaints include the alleged provision of hair and makeup services to Trump and other officials at party expense, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump’s former chief of staff.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Those allegations put a concrete question beneath the factional spectacle: whether an organization funded to elect Republicans was also used to subsidize the president’s political entourage and reward a well-connected family member. An audit could establish what was authorized, by whom and for what party purpose. Leaked emails and opposition research, by contrast, suggest that rival camps are trying to control the damage before any formal accounting controls the narrative.

The dispute follows what the AP described as the Republican Party’s worst midterm showing in a generation. Yet the backlash has not produced a broad break with Trump or his policies. Republican leaders in Washington have largely remained behind him, including on policies the AP characterized as deeply unpopular. Their emerging objection is narrower: who manages the institution, who receives its resources and who will control its machinery heading into 2028.

The White House answers dissent with leverage

The White House’s reported response exposes the actual hierarchy. It is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if RNC rebels refuse to fall in line, according to the AP. That is not an argument about whether the spending was defensible. It is the use of financial power to deter an internal examination.

The committee formally belongs to the party, but the reported threat shows how thoroughly access to money can enforce presidential control. Members may demand an audit; the White House can make resistance expensive. The rebellion is therefore real but constrained: officials are challenging Trump’s chairman while the Trump operation retains leverage over the resources they need.

Calling this merely a Republican “civil war” risks turning an institutional conflict into entertainment. The consequential issue is not that party officials are trading embarrassing material. It is that a president’s political operation can reportedly answer questions about party spending by threatening the questioners’ fundraising support.

A succession fight disguised as an accounting fight

The contest will also shape the 2028 Republican nomination, the AP reported. Control of the RNC means influence over donors, staff, party rules and the infrastructure awaiting the next presidential field. The audit demand concerns past spending, but the struggle is also about who inherits the machinery Trump has dominated.

That helps explain why the midterm losses did not automatically loosen his grip. Electoral defeat can weaken a leader without dismantling the network of appointments, money and institutional dependencies built around him. Republican officials may blame management and alleged luxuries because those targets are safer than confronting the political direction imposed from the top.

The result is a selective revolt: anger at the steward, continued submission to the principal.

The pre-election fight over federal power

AlterNet also pointed to warnings issued before the midterms about Trump’s attempts to expand federal involvement in election administration. In June, Common Cause senior policy director Dan Vicuña argued that some of those efforts were illegal, citing attempted voter-identification requirements involving independent agencies and an executive order affecting the United States Postal Service.

Common Cause was challenging that order in court. Vicuña contended that neither the president nor the Postal Service had the legal authority to turn the agency into a national election-administration body or add barriers to voting by mail. Those were his legal claims, not a reported court ruling on the executive order described.

That dispute is distinct from the RNC spending battle, but it supplies relevant context. Before the election, Trump’s allies were defending efforts to extend presidential influence into election administration. After losing badly, much of the party still declined to reconsider his leadership. The immediate rupture instead formed around internal spending and control of the next nomination cycle.

The leaked emails and personal opposition research make the revolt look ugly. The more revealing conduct is cleaner and more institutional: alleged benefits flowing through the party organization, a demand to inspect the books, and a White House prepared to use fundraising power to stop the challenge from spreading.

item.title: Kaitlan Collins peels back curtain on 'uncharacteristically silent' Trump
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump remained publicly silent after a rare nationwide ground stop stranded thousands of travelers on Friday, even as he continued posting about Gavin Newsom, a New Orleans riverboat crash, the entertainment industry and Hannibal Lecter. His administration offered a theory for the absence—Trump was letting subordinates lead—but the reporting establishes no reason for why a president usually eager to dominate the news declined to address a disruption of the national aviation system. CNN Wh
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump remained publicly silent after a rare nationwide ground stop stranded thousands of travelers on Friday, even as he continued posting about Gavin Newsom, a New Orleans riverboat crash, the entertainment industry and Hannibal Lecter. His administration offered a theory for the absence—Trump was letting subordinates lead—but the reporting establishes no reason for why a president usually eager to dominate the news declined to address a disruption of the national aviation system.

CNN White House reporter Kaitlan Collins highlighted the contrast as airports dealt with the fallout and federal officials faced questions about the system failure. The White House then issued a travel photo lid for Saturday, signaling that no public appearance by Trump was expected.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The president posted, just not about the crisis

Trump was not entirely out of communication. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said he had spoken with the president by phone and in the Oval Office. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said he had talked with him.

That makes the administration’s predicament more revealing, not less. Trump was reportedly engaged enough to speak privately with Cabinet officials and active enough to publish on Truth Social, yet he did not use his public platform to explain what had happened, reassure stranded travelers or describe the federal response.

Collins called the silence “uncharacteristic,” an assessment supported by Trump’s well-established preference for placing himself at the center of major events. The New York Times likewise noted his absence as the aviation crisis unfolded. Former Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene sharpened the criticism, writing on X that while people feared the country might be under attack, “Trump didn’t even bother to address the nation.”

The headline’s promise of a curtain being pulled back goes further than the available facts. Collins documented the president’s conspicuous absence and the subjects he chose to discuss instead. She did not establish why he stayed silent.

Delegation became the official explanation

Mullin portrayed Trump’s nonappearance as evidence of executive discipline.

“This is what President Trump does,” he said at Friday’s news conference. “He puts leaders in place, and he allows them to lead.”

That defense asks the public to treat presidential silence as a management philosophy. But the administration still relied on Trump’s presumed authority to strengthen its message: Duffy said the president wanted the full force of the federal government directed toward fixing the problem. Trump’s aides invoked his commitment while Trump avoided making it himself.

Delegating technical work to an agency secretary is ordinary governance. Leaving subordinates to account publicly for a nationwide emergency is a separate choice. Nothing about permitting Duffy to manage the response prevented Trump from addressing the people affected by it.

The arrangement also protected the president from immediate scrutiny. Duffy and Mullin stood before cameras, explained the administration’s actions and absorbed questions about the failure. Trump retained the power of the office while outsourcing its public accountability.

A funding demand without Republican ownership

Duffy called on Congress to provide another $50 billion to repair the nation’s aviation infrastructure. Reporters pressed him on an obvious political complication: Republicans had controlled Congress for the previous two years while a Republican occupied the White House.

The funding request may identify a real need, but it does not erase control of the institutions responsible for meeting it. An administration cannot plausibly present federal neglect as an external force when its own party has held the legislative and executive power needed to set priorities, appropriate money and oversee the system.

Trump’s silence helped keep that contradiction at the level of a Cabinet news conference. Duffy had to demand more money and answer for Republican stewardship; the president did neither.

A lower profile after electoral defeat

The Times connected Trump’s reduced visibility to Republicans’ significant losses in the 2026 midterm elections, reporting that he had maintained a somewhat lower profile since then. That context offers a possible political explanation, but not a confirmed account of his conduct during the ground stop.

What the episode does show is a selective retreat. Trump had not stopped broadcasting his interests or attacking political targets. He had stopped short of attaching himself publicly to a crisis that raised questions about federal capacity and Republican governance.

By the time AlterNet published its report, the president had found room in his public commentary for Hannibal Lecter but not for the thousands of Americans stranded by a nationwide aviation shutdown. His aides called that leadership through delegation. For the officials sent to face the cameras—and for the travelers waiting in airports—it looked more like authority without exposure.

item.title: Kellyanne Conway gets torched for trying to blame FAA shutdown on Democrats
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Kellyanne Conway blamed Democrats for Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop because none voted for the Republican spending package that included roughly $12.5 billion for aviation infrastructure. The accusation collapses under the governing facts: Republicans controlled Congress and the White House, passed the bill without Democratic votes, and signed it into law. Eleven days after a Democratic wave in the 2026 midterms, the party still awaiting power was being assigned responsibility for a failur
item.content:encoded:
Kellyanne Conway blamed Democrats for Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop because none voted for the Republican spending package that included roughly $12.5 billion for aviation infrastructure. The accusation collapses under the governing facts: Republicans controlled Congress and the White House, passed the bill without Democratic votes, and signed it into law. Eleven days after a Democratic wave in the 2026 midterms, the party still awaiting power was being assigned responsibility for a failure under the government Republicans ran.

The precise cause of the November 13 ground stop remained unresolved as of the reporting. That uncertainty did not stop Conway and outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson from presenting Democratic opposition as the answer. Their argument replaced an investigation into an operational breakdown with a partisan alibi.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Conway turns a Republican law into a Democratic liability

“This has been made a partisan issue,” Conway said on Fox News, before making it one herself. She argued that because no Democrat supported the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” every Democrat had effectively voted against the FAA money it contained.

That is an expedient distortion of how legislation works. Democrats opposed a much larger package that, according to AlterNet, included significant reductions to food stamps, Medicare and Medicaid. Conway stripped one provision from that package and pretended lawmakers had received a clean choice between financing the FAA and refusing to do so.

She said Democrats could have “honed in” on the aviation funding and supported the bill. But Republicans did not need their support to enact it. They secured the votes, passed the package and obtained the president’s signature. Conway’s complaint therefore was not that Democrats blocked the funding. They did not. It was that Democrats declined to endorse the Republican majority’s preferred combination of FAA investment and cuts to social programs.

The distinction matters because congressional majorities control what reaches the floor and how provisions are bundled. Republicans exercised that power, then treated the minority party’s refusal to ratify their choices as responsibility for the result.

Johnson rejects scrutiny before the cause is known

Several lawmakers called for investigations into the ground stop and questioned why the $12.5 billion had not produced the improvements the Transportation Department said it would. Johnson dismissed that demand on Fox News.

“We don’t really need any investigation to understand we need further investment,” he told Kayleigh McEnany, even though the cause of the disruption had not been established. He also claimed Democrats had negotiated FAA funding below what Republicans wanted.

That response substitutes a funding demand for a factual account. More investment may be necessary, but necessity does not explain what failed, who knew about the vulnerability or whether money already appropriated was directed effectively. Declaring the lesson before determining the cause protects the officials responsible for administering the system from the scrutiny needed to reach that lesson.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy had already acknowledged that the enacted sum was inadequate. According to the report, Duffy said before passage that $12.5 billion would not be enough; after the ground stop, he put the need closer to $50 billion. That leaves an obvious question for the administration and the Republican Congress: if they believed the system required four times the enacted amount, why did their law provide less?

A governing failure becomes an opposition talking point

The backlash to Conway’s remarks was blunt because the contradiction was plain. Political commentator Joanne Carducci noted that Republicans held Congress and the White House. Former House candidate Jeffrey Sites likewise faulted the Republican majority, while another critic described Duffy’s escalating request as an admission that the administration had underfunded the repair and was searching for someone else to blame.

Online anger does not establish the cause of the FAA failure. It does expose the weakness of the Republican defense. Democrats neither administered the Transportation Department nor prevented the bill from becoming law. The officials with authority over aviation policy, appropriations and implementation were Republicans.

The November 2026 election had already punished the governing party amid an affordability crisis that AlterNet linked in part to cuts embedded in the same legislation Conway invoked. Her response was to convert those cuts into background noise, isolate the FAA provision and demand that Democrats share ownership of a law they opposed and Republicans enacted.

An investigation could determine what caused the ground stop and whether the administration’s spending addressed the right problems. Johnson’s answer was that no investigation was needed. Conway’s was that the question belonged to Democrats. Neither explanation accounted for the elementary fact that Republicans held the power to write the bill, pass it, fund the agency and run the department when the system stopped.
